is: has he reflected on that, and, if so, how does he see himself progressing
consideration of t hose funding and financing tools, in particular to meet the apparent
fiscal hole that he has in his transport plan?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Thank you to the memb er for
those questions. The first question was in regards to public transport, and, as outlined in
the draft Government policy statement on transport, there is, I think, up to $2.3 billion
allocated to public transport services as part of that draft Govern ment policy statement.
That is an adequate activity range class to ensure investment in the public transport
services that New Zealanders need in order to make sure we are getting people where
they need to go, particularly in our larger urban centres where we need to make sure we’re
tackling congestion. And so that’s a really important part of the draft Government policy
statement on transport.
I acknowledge the question also was in regards to concessions and I would note that
there are a range of concessi ons which still exist in place which Auckland Transport,
Wellington, and Christchurch have all put in place, and there will continue to be
concessions for those people. The Government will continue to support SuperGold, Total
Mobility, and Community Connect for people who have community services cards, and
there will continue to be concessions for those on tertiary students, students, and children
as well. And so there will continue to still be support for those people.
Second question was in relation to th e Clean Car Discount scheme, and I would note
he didn’t talk about the tax side of the equation in terms of the question. The ute tax—the
ute tax—of course, this was the reverse Robin Hood scheme that the last Government
thought was the best thing. Ultimately, though, I think what the last Government did was
very good for Elon Musk. Elon Musk did very well out of it. I think it was something like
$115 million of subsidies for Elon Musk. But the reality is this was also punishing our
3000 Annual Review Debate 1 May 2024
farmers, and so we have axed the ute tax because, ultimately —and also, the other thing
about that scheme: entirely financially unsustainable. Over $300 million of taxpayers’
money put into the scheme—over $300 million of taxpayers’ money put into that scheme,
which could have gon e to health, education, law and order, all of those other priorities.
But instead the last Government thought subsidising people to buy a Tesla or a Porsche
or some other type—they’re all good cars; they’re great, but the reality is that’s how the
last Government prioritised that. People can make those choices and people will continue
to make those choices, but that’s what the last Government chose to do instead; hundreds
of millions of dollars.
The third question, in regards to the Climate Emergency Response Fund (CERF), and
the advice is that, ultimately, there’s a range of different initiatives which fell within the
CERF. Ultimately, this Government is taking the view that the emissions trading scheme
needs to do the heavy lifting when it comes to our emissions—[Interruption]

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Can I just ask for a little bit of order.
Interjections are fine, but the Minister might be answering questions that somebody wants
to know the answer to. So interjections  are fine, but it’s just too constant. Thank you.
Honourable Minister, keep going.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. Finally, asking about roading
projects and, of course, it’s great to be talking about roading projects once agai n. As
outlined in the draft Government policy statement on transport, we will be looking at all
funding and financing mechanisms in order to deliver the infrastructure that New
Zealanders need, just like they do in other countries.

items.speaker: Hon JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Thank you so much for that
contribution, Minister. I am really looking forward to hearing from the Minister of
Transport because he has repeatedly stated that there was insufficient investment in
highways and roads under the last Government.
I wonder if the Minister could enlighten the committee, for the year under financial
review, what the top three activity classes were in terms of percentage of the National
Land Transport Fund. Can he confirm that State highway improvements were the No. 3
investment under the previous Government —that almost $1 billion was spent on State
highway improvements just in the financial year under review, not including the New
Zealand Upgrade Programme, and that the only two activity classes that exceeded that, at
20 percent and 18 percent, were State highway maintenance and local road maintenance,
and that, therefore, the vast majority of the transport budget under the previous
Government was being spent on highways and local roads?

items.speaker: Grant McCallum
items.text: What about new highways?

items.speaker: Hon JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: New roads was the third-highest activity class, and I
will say for the benefit of the National member of the Transport and Infrastructure
Committee, who signed off this very report—

items.speaker: Tangi Utikere
items.text: The deputy chair.

items.speaker: Hon JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: —deputy chair—that the vast majority of the transport
budget under the previous Labour Government was spent on highways and local roads;
that, in fact, nearly $1 billion was spent on State highway improvements. And while the
Minister goes on and on about one raised pedestrian crossing in Auckland, not even
3 percent—not even 3 percent—of the transport budget was spent on walking and cycling
improvements. Can he confirm that those are in fact the numbers —that, under the last
Labour Government, whic h supposedly spent so much on alternatives to cars, in fact
only 3 percent of the transport budget was spent on walking and cycling, and that a tiny
percentage was spent on public transport relative to new State highways?
Although I know the National Party  cannot help but believe in their own talking
points that have nothing to do with reality, in fact, if the Minister is truly committed to
1 May 2024 Annual Review Debate 3001
the transport improvements that he says he is, how does he expect people to respond to
a congestion charge or a toll i f there is not sufficient investment in public transport or
safe walking and cycling infrastructure in our urban areas? What is his plan to give
people actual choice?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON B ROWN
items.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I
appreciate the member the Hon Julie Anne Genter outlining some of the elements of the
annual review report that was from the Transport and Infrastructure Committee. I would
point her to page 29 of the  draft Government policy statement on transport, which
invests in public transport services, public transport infrastructure, and walking and
cycling improvements.

items.speaker: Hon JULIE AN NE GENTER
items.text: Can the Minister of Transport
confirm that the amount in the draft Government policy statement which he has just referred
to is only 1 percent of the transport budget on walking and cycling improvements, and a
lower percentage than in the previous year, which was still a minority of the transport
budget on public transport? And now we’re in a situation where New Zealand has the
highest car ownership in the entire world because people don’t have a choice because
of decades of insufficient investment in alternatives that people would be happy to use, that
would do more for the people who need to use the roads, and that would do more to move
people and goods efficiently. To now invest in alternatives to having to own so many
cars and spend literally billions, tens of billions of dollars—

items.speaker: Grant McCallum
items.text: People in the regions need roads.

items.speaker: Hon JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: No one is questioning whether or not people in the
regions need roads. The question is : what is the best investment to move people and
goods now and that reduces the cost burden of transport on businesses and people in
New Zealand? Does the Minister understand that the best way to move more people and
goods now is to invest in better public  transport, and walking and cycling in our urban
areas, and inter -city rail and buses and ferries in the rest of our country, so that the
people using the roads don’t have to compete with so many other cars and trucks? The
single most inconvenient thing fo r someone trying to drive somewhere is not someone
on a bike, it’s not someone on public transport; it’s the other cars and trucks that are
clogging up our roads and damaging the roads, along with extreme weather events
which are caused by carbon emissions . By the way, one of our single largest sources of
carbon emissions is our transport system. What is the plan to change that?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: I thank the member the Hon Julie
Anne Genter for her question, and I would just note that page 29 of the draft Government
policy statement—and I’m happy to give her a copy—does include investment in public
transport services, does include investment in public transpo rt infrastructure, and does
include investment in walking and cycling improvements. On this side of the House,
we think we should be investing in a range of transport modes. The reality is that, for the
last six years, we’ve had a Government —ex-Government—which used to say, “We’re
going to build Auckland light rail, and we’re going to start it in 2021.” Well, they had
six years and nothing happened. The last National Government started the City Rail
Link, and it’s soon going to be completed, and that is $5 billion of investment into our
rail network in Auckland, which is going to unlock significant opportunities for
Aucklanders wanting to use public transport.
So I am incredibly proud of our track record of delivering in public transport
infrastructure, beca use we actually got stuff started and we will get things done. I am
incredibly proud of our track record when it comes to building roads, because we
started it and we will get things done. The last Government spent an awful lot of time
talking about things , talking about Auckland light rail, spending $227 million on
business case reports and consultancy reports and glossy documents and no delivery —
3002 Annual Review Debate 1 May 2024
absolutely no delivery. The members opposite say, “Well, what about Auckland?”
Well, what Aucklanders want and what Aucklanders voted for is delivery, and that is
what this Government is focused on .

items.speaker: TANGI UTIKERE
items.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I still
haven’t heard from the Minister whether or not he accepts that the Clean Car Discount’s
initiative did increase the uptake of electric vehicles —that was the question that I asked
and he still has neglected to address that.
Can I just turn to this issue of congestion charging, because it is something the Minister
has brought up in his contributions already. He did, to be fair, note it in the hearing that
congestion was a particular challenge in front of the committee. I’m interested to hear what
progress has been made with mechanisms that seek to address congestion reduction, whether
that’s congestion charging or whether that’s tolling; where the Minister sees these particular
mechanisms might work, where they would be applied, and what rationale he might have for
such locations at this stage. It’s also pleasing to hear that he’s certainly not pushing back on
the fiscal hole of between $8 billion and $22 billion for him to deliver his National Party roads
of significance there—so that’s interesting to hear.
The other is around rail. Now, in the draft Government policy statement (GPS) there
is little comment on rail —in particular, inter-regional rail. Does the Minister agree that
the investment in rail that’s subject to th is period needs to be sustained at the same or at
an increased level of investment for the period that’s under review? Does he also
agree that the levels of projected funding to support the long -term future of what is the
lower North Island rail package —for Manawatū, Wairarapa, and Kāpiti lines —are
sufficient to ensure the completion of that package in its entirety; and whether he’s
committed to ensuring that that is tagged funding? And, alongside that, his commitment
or otherwise around Te Huia service bet ween the Waikato and Auckland, which is
partway through a five-year funding opportunity.
Can I just have one more question which is around the suggestion of moving things
off the road and the Minister’s view around coastal shipping, particularly around
freight? That’s been the subject of questions in this House. It is still relevant to the
draft GPS around land transport, even though it is part of the blue highway; and
whether or not he sees there is a role of support for coastal shipping in order to
efficiently move freight off the roads, off rail, into other areas of the community,
provide some resilience capacity for communities as well.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Thank you, Madam Chair, and
I thank the member for the range of questions. I believe we’ve already answered the
member’s questions in regards to the Clean Car Discount. It’s very good and effective at
subsidising people’s choices, and ultimately, they can make those choices themselves and,
actually—so I’ve already commented on that.
In terms of congestion charge; time-of-use charging. As noted in the draft Government
policy statement (GPS), there is work under way on that in a range of other revenue
reforms.
In terms of the lower North Island —the rail improvement —that is noted on page 13
of the draft GPS as being a priority for this Government and to be funded from a
combination of Crown grants, National Land Transport Fund, and local share
contributions.
In regards to Te Huia, that is a matter for the New Zealand Transport Agency board,
ultimately, in terms of deciding what to do with that particular service. It was funded,
I think, as a trial. Ultimately the board will make a decision as part of the mid-point review
as to what should happen there next.
In terms of coastal shipping, I think I’ve had this question asked of me before and I think
the clue’s in the name. When you call something the “National Land Transport Fund”, you
1 May 2024 Annual Review Debate 3003
sort of think the “Land” part could be quite important—so the clue’s in the name. So the
coastal shipping is on the water —the coastal shipping’s on the water —and this is the
National Land Transport Fund. So I know the last Government was very keen—and there’s
a lot that can be done to support coastal shipping without simply—

items.speaker: Tangi Utikere
items.text: Just not from your Government.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: —well, without just putting money to something. This is
the problem the last Government had: everything needed to have money put into it. When,
ultimately, actually, if you look at one of one of the biggest challenges facing shipping in
New Zealand right now is the fact that the Port of Tauranga can’t get a consent for an
additional berth. Because of that, they have sh ips waiting to get into that port to be able
to load and unload their cargo.
So there are many other things we can be doing as a Government to actually make the
ability to—for our supply chains to work more efficiently, and most of it actually means
getting the red and green tape out of the way rather than just simply throwing money at a
problem. So that’s the focus of our Government: let’s fix the consenting framework, let’s
actually make sure we’re able to —for our ports to be able to operate efficiently. Those
connections to our ports are really important: that’s where the roads of national significance
are really, really important.
Actually, the market will determine what is the most efficient means in order to move
that freight. I know there are a lot of  companies which are looking at how they
move their freight. There’s an awful lot of freight which is moved on coastal shipping
already via many of the foreign shipping lines which come in port and go down the
country and  back up again. So these are proble ms which we think that we need to do
and take a different approach in order to achieve those outcomes rather than just simply
throwing money at the problem.

items.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD
items.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. It’s
been a great debate so far, looking back. I’m keen to hear from the Minister of Transport
around the Auckland regional fuel tax. I’m keen to know how much was collected by the
previous Government on it, what it was spent on, and how much was unspent. I’m keen
to know, really, did it achieve what it was set up to achieve or did it just punish more
Aucklanders at the pump?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: I thank the member for that
question. That was a fuel tax put in place by the last Government, effectively charging
Aucklanders an extra 11.5c per litre every time they filled up their car.
Ultimately, when the fuel tax was put in place, Aucklanders were told this was going
to build Mill Road —major infrastructure projects like that. Well, it raised, I think,
something like $700  million or $750 million, and it spent about $450 million. There
was about $300 million unspent when we came into Government. So about $300 million
actually raised from Aucklanders —about two years’ worth of Auckland regional fuel
tax had been collected off Aucklanders but hadn’t actually been spent. So that’s one
problem with the regional fuel tax.
Instead of people getting Mill Road, every time they filled up their car, they thought
they were filling up their car and they’d get Mill Road built a bit faster, actually they
get a speed bump. And not jus t one but dozens and dozens of them across Auckland,
which were, of course, costing—and I know my colleague from the Green Party doesn’t
like me saying this, but one of them costing $490,000.

items.speaker: Tom Rutherford
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: $490,000. So the reality is Aucklanders were being taxed
more to be slowed down, rather than to get actual infrastructure delivered. And so, of
course, on coming to Government, we passed legislation. The tax will end on 1 July —
two months from today.
3004 Annual Review Debate 1 May 2024

items.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK
items.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you.
I will take a short call and I have some specific questi ons to ask the Minister about
transport projects in the South Island, because I think I might be the first member to speak
tonight from the South Island.

items.speaker: Shanan Halbert
items.text: Not many, if any.

items.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK
items.text: Yeah, exactly. If yo u look at the new Government policy
statement, you’ll see there are not many, if any projects in the South Island.

items.speaker: Grant McCallum
items.text: Ashburton Bridge.

items.speaker: Hon Matt Doocey
items.text: Can’t you read?

items.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK
items.text: I can read—very well, actually. And there are two—there are
two. One of which is in my electorate, the Hope bypass. The question is—

items.speaker: Grant McCallum
items.text: Oh, there you go. What are you complaining about? What’s your
problem? Congratulate the mayor.

items.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK
items.text: It’s really interesting when people think they know about my
electorate; you’re welcome to come and have a look and I’ll show you around.
My comment is around the fact that we had two projects in the previous Government
policy statement because our regional transport committee had identified two priority
projects, one of which is the Hope bypass, and I’ve just referenced that the reason the
Hope bypass was needed in the first place was that there was a significant amount of
housing expansion put in place by the Tasman District Council in the previous National
Government as a housing area, and no transport plan. I was shocked when I became
the member to discover there was literally no plan. So we worked quite hard over the
last three years to get the plan and to get it into the GPS. Very concerned on that project
to see that it’s actually going to be consented three years later than was originally
planned—so not being consented until around 2026, not being built until around
2029, which is a lot later than what we had planned. So I’d like to know, Minister, why
is this project being delayed?

items.speaker: Hon Matt Doocey
items.text: Because you cancelled all the roads for six years.

items.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK
items.text: And the second question —Mr Doocey—is the Rocks Road
project, which has been—[Interruption]

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Ms Genter! Ms Genter! Please resume your
seat. OK, we’re just going to have some order here. Sorry, Rachel Boyack, we’re just
going to have some order. We know that transport is one of those touchy subjects. But if
we want to get the best out of the Minister, interjections are fine, but it would be good if
we could actually just ask the questions and let the Minister answer them and have fewer
interjections rather than shouting matches, and it’s not appropriate to get out of one’s seat
to go and have an argument with somebody on the other side.

items.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK
items.text: So I’d like to be able to just tell the story. I’ll tell the story about
Rocks Road. One of the things that we did, it had always been connected to another transport
project in Nelson, which meant we’d only get it if the Southern Link was built. We separated
it out for a reason: so that we could actually look specifically at that project.
One of the issues we have —my question to the Minister —is we have cyclones, we
have floods in Nelson, and that road closes. The residents of Nelson who came to a
public meeting of mine that I held last week said to me what if t hey were told when
their houses were flooding to travel to inner city Nelson using that road to get to safety
and it was closed. What is the Minister going to do about the resilience of Rocks Road,
which is over 100 years old and constantly closes? Why is it not in the GPS or in any
of the documents from Waka Kotahi? And what is he going to assure the people of
Nelson that he will do to improve the safety and resilience of that road?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: I thank the member for her
questions and I note there are a number of projects in the South Island which are a priority:
1 May 2024 Annual Review Debate 3005
the Hope bypass, the Ashburton Bridge, and the Woodend-Belfast—the Pegasus motorway
and Woodend bypass. I’d also make the point that actually there is proposed investment
around improvements around bridges which is a critically important issue in the South
Island, and also the increased maintenance which is not only critically important to our
roading network across New Zealand but for our State highway network and the resilience
that is that is needed, particularly in the South Island.
In terms of the issue in regards to Rocks Road, I mean, ultimately the New Zealand
Transport Agency Board is r esponsible for the prioritisation of projects which are
put forward.

items.speaker: Rachel Boyack
items.text: Based on your GPS?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Yeah, and we have outlined the roads of national
significance as being a priority within the GPS. But ultimately, the board of the New
Zealand Transport Agency needs to make decisions looking at what all the priorities are
and what has been put forward by the regional land transport plans and from the councils,
and ultimately that is the board’s decision to weigh those issues up.

items.speaker: Hon SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: Point of order, Madam
Chairperson. A few minutes ago there was an incident that occurred in this Chamber, in
this committee, that I have never seen before; it was unprecedented in my experience in
this Chamber. I invite you to report back to the Speaker about th e actions that took
place. To have a member rise from her seat, stride across the House, and then confront in
a most intimidating manner a member of this Chamber, I think, is utterly unparliamentary
and warrants further investigation and sanction.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Thank you, Mr Simpson. I will undertake to
take that course of action. Thank you.

items.speaker: GRANT McCALLUM
items.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. I’d just
like to address to the Minister the opportunity cost that’s arisen from the lack of the roads
of national significance programme after the last few years. We recently had a study done
in Northland which showed that in excess of $2 billion of benefits potentially could come
to the Northland economy with a four-lane highway to the North, and we’ve recently seen
the Brynderwyns, which were going to be opened in a couple of weeks, suffer a significant
collapse. So what would be the impact of a decent roads of national significance
programme for this country and for the provinces, like Northland?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Well, I thank the member for the
question. I acknowledge that it is tough for Northlanders right now with the Brynderwyns
closed. That is a really important part of our State highway network, but I also acknowledge
that the Mangamukas are also closed due to resilience issues. The New Zealand Transport
Agency chose to close it on the basis that that was the most efficient and cost-effective and
safe way to be able to make critical improvements to extend the life of that roading project
by somewhere up to seven to 10 years.
So I have 100 percent support for the agency’s decision on that, yet I also accept that it’s
had a huge impact on Northland and the impact of having to go on those detours. The news
we heard today that that is going to be closed for longer is not great, but, ultimately, that is
why we have, as a Government, outlined Whangārei to Auckland as a road of national
significance which is really, really important for resilience but also for economic growth
and productivity. We’ve seen the benefits that the Waikato Expressway has brought to the
Waikato and to Auckland, and the economic growth and productivity opportunities that that
has presented, and we see those opportunities for Northland as well. S o the agency is
working at pace around that, looking at funding and financing options, what that may look
like, but, ultimately, it is critically important that we work at pace on that route due to the
serious resilience issues of that existing road as well.
3006 Annual Review Debate 1 May 2024
GREG O’CONNOR (Labour —Ōhāriu): Thank you, Madam Chair. The Minister
spoke of the range of activities in his purview as Minister. One of them, of course, is under
the Civil Aviation Authority and air traffic. Is he aware that where there are changes to
flight paths notified under what’s called a DMAP system —which is divergent missed
approach protection system—that there are obligations which must be met by the agencies,
particularly around consultation and notification? Has he been briefed on where those
obligations have not been met, particularly in relation to changes at Wellington Airport and
proposed changes which are about to take place at Auckland Airport?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Yes, I’m aware of those
obligations. I’m not 100 percent sure right now whether—I don’t think I’ve been briefed
on those specific changes, recently, but I’ll certainly go and ask for one.
GREG O’CONNOR (Labour —Ōhāriu): Well, perhaps if I can clarify: have you
been briefed on breaches to those obligations to notify and to consult?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Not that I’m aware of, but I’ll go
and double-check.

items.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
items.text: Oh, thank you —good
choice, Madam Chair. Look, I’ve got a question to the Minister about the very important
motorway proposed from Belfast to Pegasus, including the Woodend Bypass, and if he
had any understanding of the original cost that was proposed when it was first announced
by the last National Government in 2017, and what is that increased cost now through six
years of inactivity, with that road being cancelled under the last Government? And
potentially his views on whether the increased costs now —that could have actually
funded other stuff in New Zealand; other roads and maintenance. And if Rachel Boyack
from Nelson believes there should have been a lot more roading projects on your list, why
do you think they weren’t built in the last six years under her Government?

items.speaker: Hon SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: Point of order. Madam Chair,
I just wanted to make it clear that my earlier intervention was a request to recall
the Speaker.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Ah, apologies. So I’ve just had that question
from the Clerks as to whether you said, “report to the Speaker”, so you’ve clarified that?

items.speaker: Hon SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: Yes, I’m sorry. I may have —
it was—

items.speaker: TANGI UTIKERE
items.text: Point of order. Just speaking to that
briefly, and, really, it’s a matter of process because I think Mr Simpson was asking
for a course of action, but the presiding officer hasn’t ruled on any course of action.
So I’m just not quite —the attempt to recall the —

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Well, my understanding, to Mr Simpson’s point
of order that I would—because the situation is now under control, that I would report what
happened back to the Speaker and then come back to the House as to what was resolved. But
I now understand that Mr Simpson was asking for something further.

items.speaker: Hon SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: Well, it was an unprecedented
incident in my experience, Madam Chair—

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I understand the point of order.

items.speaker: Hon SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: —and so I’m a little bit in the hands of the committee. But
I think that the incident warranted an intervention, and I unders tand that the process of
the House requires intervention to occur as soon as is practical after an incident.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: OK, yep.

items.speaker: Hon SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It was a serious, intimidatory physical attack upon another
member in this Chamber and that’s unacceptable.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: So I have got advice here from the Clerk, just
on that point of order, that if a member wants to recall the Speaker by convention, that
1 May 2024 Annual Review Debate 3007
the Speaker can be recalled. So, at this point, we would ask for the Speaker to be recalled,
please. Sorry to Mr Simpson, I misunderstood what you said.
Debate interrupted.
House resumed.
Speaker Recalled

items.speaker: Hon SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I’ve
asked you to be recalled to the Chair because of an incident that took place a few minutes
ago during the hearings that the committee was involved with. Rachel Boyack was
speaking, and then an interjection and an interaction occurred between my colleague the
Hon Matt Doocey, sitting down here, and the Hon Julie Anne Genter, where the honourable
member Julie Anne Genter strode across the Chamber of the House and physically accosted
Minister Doocey in a threatening, intimidatory way that I think is utterly unbecoming and
unparliamentary of this Chamber.
I’ve never seen behaviour of that sort in this Chamber in my time in this House. I think
it’s a serious matter that warrants an intervention immediately, and that the member is still
sitting in this Chamber without having apologised or accounted for her actions is, I think,
intolerable and needs your intervention.
Further, I’m advised that the footage is clearly available on the parliamentary
video facility.

items.speaker: SPEAKER
items.text: Therefore, publicly available as well.

items.speaker: STEVE ABEL
items.text: May I speak? I was not in the Chamber at the time, but I did
see the end of the alleged incident on Parliament TV upstairs. I did not see any contact
between the member and the member across—and I appreciate you nodding your head to
that. There was no physical contact.
I understand from my colleague that she feels strongly about the issue and wanted
to show the member the actual data in a booklet. She’s a very science - and data - driven
human being and she was wanting to show him the actual information in the booklet,
and when there was an intervention immediately by the Chair —Barbara Kuriger —
the member then, rightly, crossed the floor and took her seat and has remained in place
since then. That is my understand ing of what happened, and I just wanted to convey
that to you, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Dr VANESSA WEENINK
items.text: All of us witnessed this
incident. At the time, whilst some of us found some aspects of it quite amusing, looking at
the situation from the perspective of there was my colleague, seated, whilst a person was
standing over him with a book, making a lot of gestures and angry—

items.speaker: Hon Scott Simpson
items.text: Loud.

items.speaker: Dr VANESSA WEENINK
items.text: —loud and quite intimidating actions, and I reflected
that had that been myself sitting there with either another female or, indeed, if a male
was doing that to me, the way that that would be viewed would be quite different. But
I feel that no matter who it was, that was an extraordinary outburst, and it was
intimidating in its nature —coming from where I was sitting.

items.speaker: Hon KAREN CHHOUR
items.text: I would like to add to that that
from my position, it looked like a huge amount of intimidation that was going on
very close to the person —standing over the person —and physically shaking a book
in that person’s face. If t hat was me, I would have felt very intimidated, and I feel that
it was really inappropriate.

items.speaker: Hon JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: If I could apologise for my
actions, Mr Sp eaker. It was the last thing I wanted to do to intimidate anyone in this
3008 Annual Review Debate 1 May 2024
House. What has absolutely motivated me is a desire to share information that I believe
would be of benefit to everyone in this House, and I’m very sorry that if in my passion to
do so, I was intimidating. That was not my intention.

items.speaker: SPEAKER
items.text: Well, it is most certainly not unusual for MPs from either side of the House
to have discussions that are quiet. They’re normally within the benches —in fact, they’re
always within the benches—because it is not appropriate for any MP to stand on the floor of
Parliament and to engage in, effectively, debate, if that’s what it was. I’m not in a position to
say that I saw it—I’m a bit like Mr Abel. I’m only listening to what I’ve heard, and it doesn’t
reflect well on Parliament when we have these sorts of moments.
I think the member has just indicated that you’re apologetic for what is, really, what
I missed, if you like, in the scheme of things. You may in a moment, when I ca ll
you— hen I call you, you might like to expand on that a little bit.
But what I do want to say to all members of the House is that if any member believes
at any point that anyone has breached the Standing Orders or breached the privilege of
the House, w hich is to speak freely and to speak in an environment where you’re
unintimidated by anybody else and in an environment where your views are challenged
only from the speaking position of the person who might like to challenge them —that
is debate. Beyond that, it becomes, potentially, something else. I’ll hear for the last time
from Julie Anne Genter.

items.speaker: Hon JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Apologies, Mr Speaker. I didn’t
hear the last thing you said—you’d hear from me?

items.speaker: SPEAKER
items.text: Oh, it was incredibly wise, so I’m sorry that you missed it. I just said that
it is totally inappropriate for there to be any actions that can in any way be considered
intimidating, so that’s where you’re at.

items.speaker: Hon JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: That is, Mr Speaker, why I’m apologising that I was
physically intimidating. It was not my intention—

items.speaker: SPEAKER
items.text: All right.

items.speaker: Hon JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: —and I will not do that in the future.

items.speaker: SPEAKER
items.text: Good. Well, we don’t want to see that happen again. If the member feels
that her passionate feelings about the matters being debated are to such a point where you
feel like you ne ed to intervene like that, I would suggest that quietly going out of the
House would be a much better solution and far more orderly than approaching anybody
in their benches.
So I’d just state again that I think we’ll now return to the committee, but if a nyone
feels as though there has been a breach of privilege, then they know that there is a course
of action to follow in that regard. The House is back in committee. The committee
is resumed.
In Committee
Debate resumed.
Transport (continued)

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: OK, I’m just going to explain, because we’ve
actually spent a little bit of time focusing on the issue that’s just occurred. The Minister
has indicated that he can stay here up until 8.40 p.m., so we will continue the committee
stage for a couple more questions, and then we’ll carry on back into the House business
after that.

items.speaker: ANDY FOSTER
items.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. Look, I have a question —
actually, it arose out of the comments, Minister, you made about coastal shipping and
innovative thinking.
The circumstances I want to draw to your attention —and this is a South Island
question, Rachel. You will all be aware of the damage that was done to the Marlborough
1 May 2024 Annual Review Debate 3009
Sounds roads in the big floods at the end of 2022. We’re now in the circumstance where
there’s a huge amount of putting them back together again and resilience work that’s
needed to be done; I’ve actually had a look at some of it. Particularly in the more extreme
Sounds area, the cost of the roading solution is actually a really, really large cost, but it
gets a subsidy. So that may, for the local council, be the cheapest option. However, the
coastal option doesn’t get a subsidy but may be a cheaper option overall for “New Zealand
Inc.”, so the combination of ratepayer and taxpayer.
So I’m drawing that to your attention and asking if that is something that you could
give consideration to and the agency could give consideration to as a lateral way of trying
to deliver the outcome at the least possible cost for the best possible benefit.

items.speaker: TANGI UTIKERE
items.text: Thank you, Madam Chair. Just
going back to the Minister’s responses around the “roads of National Party significance”
and the $30 billion to $46 billion cost, it really is embarrassing that only three of them relate
to the South Island. I know the Minister’s very generous in terms of his time this evening
but he’s just not giving in the spirit to the mainlanders.
I do want to move on to two other areas. The first is road safety and speed. I wonder
if the Minis ter can hear my question —either Minister. There was acceptance in the
hearing, by Waka Kotahi, that the strategy and approach that had decreased the level
of road deaths to date, which was currently the lowest it had been in the last five years
despite the traffic volumes on the network increasing by 6 percent during that time —
and was wanting to know how that strategy or approach aligns with the Government’s
approach to speed reduction initiatives. On the DSI stat —or the death and serious
injury statistics—how have they informed the Minister’s decision -making approach to
speed reductions in that particular space? And then also whether he accepts or not that
road safety is a primary consideration in this space and what advice he’s either sought or
advice he has received about the impact of increasing speed limits on road crash numbers,
on fatalities, and really looking at what that priority level looks like.
The final point I want to ask the Minister a question about is around drivers’ licences
and whether he agrees, as was placed in front of the committee, that there are, in fact,
inequities when it comes to Māori members of the community, but also actually around
Pacific and new migrants, and, if so, what specific actions he is taking to address those
transport inequities for them that’s actually referenced in the select committee report, and
how the specific barriers around licensing for either new drivers or relicensed drivers
might actually be overcome as a result of some of the work that he has planned.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: I just want to thank members for
their questions. I note my colleague the Hon Matt Doocey asked about the Belfast to Pegasus
motorway and Woodend bypass. I think, when it was initially proposed, it was something
around $100 million, I think—the project—$120 million. Of course, that was some time ago.
The reality is the fact that that was not delivered under the last Government but was cancelled
will mean those costs have gone up, and that ultimately means we are delivering less as a
Government. The last Government makes it more challenging to deliver other projects now
due to that increased cost, so we are left with the significant challenges that we have in terms
of the pipeline of projects that are needed.
In terms of member Andy Foster and his question around the issue in Marlborough,
I acknowledge the challenges there. Ultimately, what we’re focused toward here is
making sure we get the agency back to core business building and maintaining the roads.
And ultimately, there’s been significant engagement between the agency and the
council in Marlborough to ensure that the appropriate response is made in terms of
addressing many of those challe nges. But I acknowledge that with these severe weather
events, they do create some difficult challenges for local communities.
3010 Annual Review Debate 1 May 2024
In relation to the question from member Tangi Utikere around safety—and, of course,
safety is one of the strategic priorities within the draft Government policy statement (GPS)
on transport, and if he was to turn to page 18 of the draft GPS he would see the significant
increase that has occurred in the last 10 years of deaths and crashes involving alcohol or
drugs. That has gone from around 100 deaths per year involving alcohol or drugs to near
200 deaths involving alcohol and drugs. And so, of course, a priority is to ensure that we
can fix the legislation regarding drug testing and progress is being made on that in drafting
that legislation. The second is in relation to increasing the number of breath tests on our
roads—a critically important thing, and I’m noting that last year I think there was close to
the target of breath tests achieved but for the previous number of years that had not been
achieved. That is a really important measure of actually trying to improve road safety, and
critically important.
Also just ensuring that we’re building the roading infrastructure that New Zealanders
need. And, of course, we’ve seen the eviden ce of, for example, the Kāpiti Expressway,
where there’s been a significant reduction in deaths and serious injuries in the Kāpiti
area following the construction of the Kāpiti Expressway. And so it’s critically
important we build the major infrastructure that New Zealanders need so people can get
where they need to go quickly and safely.

items.speaker: Hon SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: I move, That the committee
report progress.
Motion agreed to.
Progress to be reported.
House resumed.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Mr Speaker, the committee has considered the
Appropriation (2022/23 Confirmation and Validation) Bill and reports progress. I move,
That the report be adopted.
Motion agreed to.
Report adopted.

sections.heading: New Zealand Superannuation And Retirement Income

items.text: (CONTROLLING INTERESTS) AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Debate resumed from 30 April.

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: We have call No. 6, which is a split call.
Te Pāti Māori have the first call. No, they’re not —so we’ll call, ah, Celia Wa de-Brown.
Excuse me, Ms Wade-Brown, I’m having an attack of “Speaker-itis”.

items.speaker: CELIA WADE -BROWN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I rise to express the
Green Party’s support for this bill, the New Ze aland Superannuation and Retirement
Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill. The Guardians of New Zealand
Superannuation perform an extremely important service for today’s superannuitants and
those fortunate enough to live to 65 in the future.
Superannuation is about the only benefit that is not means -tested, and that near -
universality is admirable. It isn’t perfect. There are complexities about how people who
are New Zealand residents who work here for years and commit their hearts to this
country can be put through the wringer because they’re not born here, or they’re born
here, but they’ve worked overseas for a few years. But that is a debate about entitlement
and equity, and about fund distribution, not investment, and thus is for another day.
1 May 2024       NZ Super. & Retire. Income (Controlling Interests) Amdt Bill 3011
Today’s debate is about widening the power of the Guardians so that they can do an
even better job within the existing economic system. It is the only economic system in the
OECD without either a capital gains tax nor a wealth tax, and I know that my colleagues
across the House really value being part of the OECD and give us great examples about
how we should follow their example in other areas.
As Treasury notes, removing the control restriction may enable the New Zealand
Superannuation Fund to access a wid er group of viable investment partners. This could
attract institutional investors who are comfortable with the Guardians’ due diligence
practices, particularly as the Guardians look for scalable investment opportunities such
as strategic infrastructure. T he Greens would question what strategic infrastructure
might be chosen. We feel, for example, that housing is an undeniable public good,
whereas new motorways may be less so, but I think we may have had enough debate on
transport for the moment.
The New Zealand Superannuation Fund has a reputation of being world leading in
environmental, social, and governance —ESG for short —integration, and it uses
its influence as a shareholder to encourage companies to manage and report on their
ESG risks. So it is help ing companies, basically, do the right thing, and often the right
thing is good for investment, too.
Now, there are several excellent exclusions. So to those people who have spoken
earlier in the debate and said, “Oh, we’ve got to be careful not to tell th em how to run
their business or what to invest in.”, let me just make a few notes of what the exclusions
are. The New Zealand Superannuation Fund does not invest in companies in the tobacco
industry, and, presumably, Minister Costello is not planning an am endment there.
Another exclusion is companies involved in the processing of whale meat. Fortunately,
whales are much larger than frogs, so I presume that they’re going to continue to be
safe, although their seabed may be trashed. Very topically, another Ne w Zealand
Superannuation Fund exclusion is companies involved in developing settlements in the
Israeli-occupied territories. The fourth example is companies involved in the
manufacture of civilian automatic and semi -automatic firearms, and, surely, Ministe r
McKee will not suggest an amendment there either.
So there is a balance between good principles encouraging better social and
environmental behaviour versus political interference in the details of investment. It is a
shame that the opportunity for stronger alignment with the Government’s goal—reiterated
in James Shaw’s valedictory tonight —of net zero carbon emissions by 2050 was not
explicitly taken. But I suspect that in the intelligent investment fund—

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: Celia Wade-Brown
items.text: I thought I might have the other half of—Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The member can ask f or leave to
complete the other half of the five minutes. She can seek leave to that effect.

items.speaker: CELIA WADE-BROWN
items.text: May I seek leave to complete the No. 6 slot?

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The member seeks leave to complete
her time. Is there any objection? There is objection.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I rise unexpectedly
because I thought I had another five minutes before I got to my feet. But, that being said, we
can adapt—that’s fine.
It’s a pleasure to speak on the New Zealan d Superannuation and Retirement Income
(Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill —which almost took up a minute. All joking
aside, this is a very important bill, and I want to push back on some of the points
just made by Celia Wade-Brown, the previous speaker. But prior to doing that, we should
talk about what the bill is about.
3012         NZ Super. & Retire. Income (Controlling Interests) Amdt Bill 1 May 2024
Actually, the New Zealand Superannuation Fund is of huge importance to New
Zealand, as a whole, and New Zealanders, in particular. We have an ageing population,
and we know that. We ha ve an issue with our finances at the moment, and having the
Superannuation Fund, which will, in time, be able to underpin our superannuation scheme
is, I think, a fantastic resource and an asset that we should ensure has all the tools it needs
to operate efficiently.
This bill allows the Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation to hold a controlling
interest in companies. Currently, they’re precluded from doing that, as I’m sure members are
aware. But if we go back and look at what they were founded under, the fund’s purpose was
to make money from investments rather than to own companies. That is one of the reasons
why they’re not able to hold a controlling interest in a company.
In the early days, I accept that that was quite a sound rationale, but nowadays  things
have grown. The fund is worth in the high $60 billion to $70 billion now. That’s a lot of
money, and that’s what we lack in our capital markets. We lack depth in our capital
markets and that means, often, that companies look offshore. Nothing wrong  with
overseas investment—I have nothing against that —but having domestic investments is
important as well.
The Guardians have invested quite significantly offshore as well, and they have a
balance of investments in all sorts of investments. They’ve got e quities and all sorts
of other investments, but having a broad portfolio is really important. But now, given
the size of the fund and that lack of capital depth in New Zealand, it is important
to allow them to be able to take an interest, which might well be a controlling interest.
That test of a controlling interest is quite interesting, because what is a controlling
interest? It’s not necessarily 51 percent, as people might think; it could be quite a bit
smaller than that. Because of the way company share holdings work, it could be as
little as 20 percent, or even less in some diverse shareholding companies, which is
quite common in equity markets.
But I note that Celia Wade-Brown—who is a member I really respect and I respect her
opinions, but I do differ on some things that that she said. Investing in strategic
infrastructure—yes, I think the problem we run into when we start prescribing what you
can and can’t invest in is that you’re then limiting choices. Limiting choices means
probably—almost certainly—limiting returns.
So we have to make a decision of do we have a superannuation fund that is something we
want to achieve political ends with, or is it something we want to secure superannuation with,
and I’d argue strongly that it should be the latter. I think we have Kiwis who have worked
hard to pay for superannuation. They are investing in their future and their family’s future,
effectively, because, with a bit of luck, they might pass something on to their people who are
their heirs and successors. So I think it’s important that we, therefore, allow the
Superannuation Fund to grow as quickly and as safely as it can, and to do that, it means that
we’d need to take a broad range of investment positions.
I think we can all agree that we don’t like investi ng in tobacco. I don’t think that’s
a good thing. I agree with that —I don’t have any issue with that, at all. But it’s a dying
industry anyway, so would you probably invest in it? It’s unlikely. Whale meat —
again, the same thing. I don’t think anyone would disagree with that —I certainly
wouldn’t. But in settlements in Israel —well, I don’t know. That’s going a bit far
away; I’m not sure  about that. Would we even invest in that, given the unrest in that
area? I  think any sound investment manager would say, “We ll, that’s not for me.”
The investment returns would have to be extreme, to say the least, to do that. Then
firearms —well, yes, but sometimes firearms are needed. Which ones are we talking
about—not sure. We’d have to prescribe that.
1 May 2024       NZ Super. & Retire. Income (Controlling Interests) Amdt Bill 3013
But I just gave a speech last week, which I know members would be very interested in,
because it was at a public accounts committee conference in Perth. My speech was on
sustainability reporting and public accounts committees’ role in that, and one of the issues
for me is when you require, say, banks and financial institutions to report on their emissions
profile—stay with me on this, Mr Speaker, it does relate to this—that—

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: As long as it’s not a travel story ,
Mr Smith.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: Well, I was just checking. Once you start prescribing that sort of
thing, you end up in a situation where—I went and I visited a farm when I was in Western
Australia that I used to work on. They’ve got a tractor tha t burns 76 litres of diesel an
hour. If they wanted to buy a more fuel-efficient tractor, electric vehicles are certainly not
an option and are nowhere in the future for that type of operation, and they’d go to their
bank and say, “I’d like some money to b uy this new tractor.” and the bank would say,
“Oh, no, we’ve got too many agricultural emissions on our books. We’re not going to
lend you any money.”
That’s the sort of thing that happens when you start prescribing what you can and what
you can’t invest in, and I think it’s so short-sighted. We haven’t thought this through. We’re
not talking about landmines here. Often, what we’re talking about is energy, which is the
blood of life, really. There’s a close relation between energy—

items.speaker: Simon Court
items.text: Crude flows in your veins, Mr Smith.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: Oh, yes. There’s a close relationship between energy and wealth,
and wealth and life expectancy, and I would say one thing about life expectancy is that
as a politician, I don’t think your life expectancy is going to be that great if you want to
reduce the li fe expectancy of your constituents. I think that is the issue with trying
to control investment decisions, and I think that the Superannuation Fund is very
well placed to make investment decisions and to make risk assessments on what their
investments shou ld or shouldn’t be. I think we should leave it at that, and that is why
I wholeheartedly support this bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon Dr DEBORAH RUSSELL
items.text: Mr Speaker, look, thank you for the
opportunity to speak on this bill. It’s a bill on which there’s widespread agreement across
the House, but there are just a few issues I would like to touch on in what will be a brief
contribution from me.
The first is just to reflect on the nickname that there was for this fund for a long time.
It was for quite a long time known as the Cullen fund because it was set up by Sir Michael
Cullen, who was a very far-sighted Minister of Finance. He gave us KiwiSaver—which has
proven a real boon to New Zealand —and also set up the New Zealand Superannuation
Fund. The objective was to assist with the payment of superannuation in the years when the
baby boomers are retiring, actually, and some of us are getting perilously close to that. So
it will assist in that payment.
It’s a sovereign wealth fund, and over the years, as the fund managers have gotten more
and more experience and more capacity to understand investing and have built up experience
within New Zealand, it has expanded what it can and can’t invest in. So this is an appropriate
move for the Cullen fund—it’s usually known as the New Zealand Superannuation Fund
now—to look to take controlling interests in firms.
Interestingly, as was recounte d in the House a couple of weeks ago by, I think,
Barbara Edmonds, who was telling a story of how Grant Robertson, when he was
Minister of Finance, put this bill together and, initially, had checked in with Sir Michael
Cullen about it, and Sir Michael did feel that it was around about appropriate for the
Cullen fund to move into this sort of position now. So the founder of the fund thought
that it was the right sort of move, and I know that across the House that is supported
now because we do want that fund  to have some good returns.
3014         NZ Super. & Retire. Income (Controlling Interests) Amdt Bill 1 May 2024
I just wanted to touch on a couple of points which other speakers have raised. One of
the earliest speakers perhaps was suggesting that we should have a think about what sort
of infrastructure the Cullen fund might invest in. I think we need to be careful, and we
need to be careful because we actually don’t want politicians interfering too closely in the
investment decisions of the Superannuation Fund. We actually need to leave the managers
to use their expertise in that area. Th ere would be a problem with inviting that much
political interference, and I think that as politicians, we ought to remain well away from
it. It is up to them to work out what are the best uses of the Superannuation Fund money
to get the best return.
However, having said that, I do have some views about the ethical investing, as well. One
of the former speakers was a little unsure that ethical investing was a suitable way to go, but,
actually, ethical investing is starting to be well developed now in terms of what funds do and
don’t invest in. There are some pretty well -established parameters, and I’m sure the
Guardians of the Superannuation Fund can continue to do well in that regard.
So this is a sensible move. It’s a move that is endorsed across the House . It’s great
to see this bill getting through its second reading, and I’m sure that it will progress
further through the House and end successfully in due course. So I commend this bill
to the House.

items.speaker: CATHERINE WEDD
items.text: It’s a pleasure to rise and speak in
support of this bill. As the member across the House, the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, has
already said, it makes sensible and practical sense, and so we certainly agree on that. It’s
all really about providing more investment opportunities throughout New Zealand, which,
of course, on this side of the House, is what we’re all about in terms of looking at
strengthening our economy and getting it back on track. This will be very positive for New
Zealand industries and infrastr ucture and really helps provide further jobs and
opportunities. So, overall, it’s a very positive move because the amendments will remove
the restriction on the New Zealand Superannuation Fund and allow it to take a controlling
stake in entities in the future.
As we’ve already heard from members, the New Zealand Superannuation Fund has been
very successful. It’s sitting at about $70 billion and is projected to reach $110 billion by the
end of the decade. It has a healthy return of 11.9 percent, and we’ve already talked about
returns and diversity and making sure that we are diversifying investments to get better
returns for New Zealanders.
We’ve heard about that diversity, and we’ve heard that the bill needs to make sure
that we are leaving it to the Guardi ans of New Zealand Superannuation to be careful
around those investments in ensuring that diversity, but the bill will also allow for the
Guardians to hold a controlling interest in a business and to take a controlling interest
in more operating companies.  This is positive because it’s removing the control
restriction, which will enable the New Zealand Superannuation Fund to access a wider
group of viable investment partners and opportunities, particularly here in New Zealand,
which is where we want to see more investment and more capital, because that’s what’s
going to help grow our economy.
Removing the control restriction, therefore, provides the Guardians with that added
extra flexibility and the ability to invest in more projects and more infrastructure, and this
approach is consistent with the Guardians’ mandate, I believe, to invest the fund on a
prudent commercial basis and, in doing so, manage the fund in a manner consistent with
best practice. That’s all about, again, that diversification of investment.
But this bill will also promote operational efficiencies, and we’re all about efficiency—
we want to see more efficiency because for the past six years, we haven’t seen a lot of
efficiency—and we will help ensure the New Zealand Superannuation Fund a ssets are
being managed in an optimal way, which is what we want to see, particularly if we’re going
1 May 2024       NZ Super. & Retire. Income (Controlling Interests) Amdt Bill 3015
to invest in the future for all New Zealanders, as we’ve already talked about, with that
ageing population. The New Zealand Superannuation Fund has shown since its inception
remarkable growth and maturity, significantly enhancing its size and its capability and
its operational model, which is a success story, and we agree with that. But there’s
obviously always room for improvement, and that is what this amendment bill is going to
achieve, by opening up for more investment in New Zealand and opening up more
opportunity for capital.
This change is pivotal for attracting institutional investors who have confidence in
the Guardians’ due diligence around investm ent acumen. When we heard, through the
select committee, the annual review of the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, they
did talk about this due diligence and they talked about the success of the investments,
but also it amplifies opportunities for domestic  investment. I think the key is the
domestic investments, because it’s all about strategic infrastructure and deepening
that capital opportunity.
I’d like to take this opportunity to look at a couple of the investments, because
we’ve got a few case studie s in the annual review here, and they look at some of the
industries that the New Zealand Superannuation Fund is investing in in New Zealand.
I was particularly interested in the agriculture investments which we’re seeing in the
sector in New Zealand, and there are dairy investments in here, there’s horticulture,
there’s viticulture and hops —

items.speaker: Dan Bidois
items.text: Fruit bowl.

items.speaker: CATHERINE WEDD
items.text: Absolutely—as we’ve already said, it is good for Hawke’s
Bay and for Tukituki, Hastings, the frui t bowl of New Zealand, because that is
where there has been some investment. There’s been investment here in our apple
orchards, in our intellectual property apple varieties, which fetch a premium in the
international markets.
This industry really needs investment at the moment, because this capital helps add value
to the produce that we export to our global markets around the world, and that’s what we’re
trying to do. It is to always fetch a higher premium for our products on the global stage.
The partnerships which they talk about in here that the New Zealand Superannuation Fund
has have given our exporters that capital to invest in global growth strategies, and it’s given
them the ability to increase per hectare returns, which, again, is very positive and is a long-
term investment in land. But it is also to introduce new orchard management techniques
and other new agriculture innovation, which all takes capital and investment. This is what
creates jobs and opportunities in our regions.
So this type of inv estment is really important and particularly at this time in our
primary industries and within our agriculture sector where they’ve been doing it very,
very tough for these past six years. It’s been very challenging, and I’m hearing all the
time that there’s a lot of red tape and regulation, and we have to remove that to get these
businesses moving. But also they want to see more access to capital, and that’s what this
comes back to, too. If we open up this opportunity, there’s going to be more access to
capital in New Zealand, which means that we’ve got a better opportunity to strengthen
our economy but also futureproof for the future in terms of New Zealanders and that
access to superannuation.
We all know we have major infrastructure needs in this country, which is another area
where we may see some benefits when it comes to financing through the Superannuation
Fund, and it’s likely that an entity like the New Zealand Superannuation Fund would in
future choose to invest in the controlling entities in these sorts of assets and in many other
assets that are targeted at infrastructure in New Zealand. We’ve already talked tonight about
the roading, and, obviously, we need better roading and infrastructure in New Zealand
3016         NZ Super. & Retire. Income (Controlling Interests) Amdt Bill 1 May 2024
because we have an infrastructure deficit. So this certainly opens up more opportunity there
for capital in terms of that investment.
But granting the New Zealand Superannuation Fund the ability to hold controlling
interests aligns with the practice of many global sovereign wealth funds that have transitioned
to managing more capital in-house as they mature. So this aligns internationally, and I think
that’s really, really important as well, because we need to be looking globally and looking
internationally, because that’s where there is opportunity.

items.speaker: Coming back to superannuation
items.text: as we all know here in New Zealand, New Zealanders
aged 65 and over receive New Zealand superannuation payments, which are paid for by
our taxpayers today. But over the next decade, the New Zealand population will age
significantly, as we’ve touched on here, and Statistics New Zealand —I just thought it
was interesting to maybe touch on a few stats, because I think that they are quite mind -
boggling when you do think about these stats and what we’re facing into the future.
During the 2020s, almost a quarter of a million more New Zealanders will reach 65 and
over and will be claiming that super, and so, by the late 2050s, they’re predicting
that we’re going to see that one in every four New Zealanders will be 65 or older. Now ,
this means that in the future, New Zealand will have more people of retirement
age as a proportion of the population than ever, ever before, and so there will be fewer
working-age people to pay tax to fund the greater cost of retirement. These projection s
have significant implications for the ability of future Governments to fund not just a
universal superannuation benefit but other vital areas such as health, welfare, education,
and law enforcement.
I’m the chair of the New Zealand Population and Development Committee, and our
population make-up here in New Zealand is changing because of our country’s fertility rate
at the moment. We have record-low birth rates. At the moment, we’ve got 1.56 births for
every woman in 2023, so our country’s fertilit y rate has been a lot lower than the
replacement rate of 2.1. I talk about this because it is actually quite relevant to what we’re
talking about, because we are seeing an ageing population where we are going to have to
think about our healthcare workers a nd the superannuation that our over -65s will be
claiming. Look, in my home region of Hawke’s Bay, 19 percent of our population there is
over 65, which is higher than the national average of 17 percent.
So this is certainly an area that we have to think ab out. Superannuation is key to the
stability of this country, and that is why I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Thank you, and I’d just say, Ms Wedd,
if you’re going to drift off the bill like you did, at least make it interesting and pertinent to
the Speaker. So thank you—and here’s a challenge for the next speaker.

items.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS
items.text: Mr Speaker, thank you for the
opportunity to take a short call on this bill —this important bill —the New Zealand
Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill,
which was shepherded through by the Hon Grant Robertson and picked up by the
Minister of Finance, Nicola Willis, and I commend them both on the excellent work
on what has become a cross -partisan thing that all New Zealanders can be proud of: a
superannuation scheme that invests directly in regional development projects. It is a
driver of economic growth in our regions and in our cities, and it’s something which
will provide for future generations in a way which is sustainable and that builds on
those things that we h old dear.
But this breakout of “Kumbaya” in the House is a little bit ironic. On this side of the
House, on these Labour benches, we believe in public ownership of strategic assets. We
believe that the Government has a role in owning things like a superan nuation scheme
which goes out there and drives economic regional development by investing in the
things we care about —by investing in our strategic industries and in making sure that
1 May 2024       NZ Super. & Retire. Income (Controlling Interests) Amdt Bill 3017
New Zealanders have access to capital in exactly the ways we have heard from members
on the Government benches tonight.
But that Government has no economic plan beyond cutting public ownership of the
services that we rely on —on the services which they are stripping 6.5 percent and
7.5 percent of all Government ownership of those services—and that flies directly in the
face of all of those speeches that we have heard tonight from that side of the House. We’ve
heard that Government ownership and that the public good is what we’re getting out of this
bill. Well, this is something which is important here, but it is not something that everyone
agrees on, and it is something that we need to think carefully about.
So let’s talk about what this bill does. It does allow the superannuation scheme to
take those investment decisions to the next level, and, as you’ve heard from my colleague
the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, this represents a shift in gear for what the superannuation
scheme can do, because when we think about these controlling interests, what do we
mean by that?
When it was set up, it had a very specific mandate to act like an investment fund with no
direct investment into companies, because it wasn’t in the business of owning specific
companies or specific pieces of infrastructure or having any sort of guardianship over specific
projects. But it has had a history in the last decade of investing in big projects which would
have otherwise not been able to go ahead without its investments—things like, in the last
National Government, large-scale housing developments.
One of those was t he Hobsonville Point development on the old airbase site.
Investment from the Superannuation Fund enabled the development of each super block
to then be sold on to developers who built houses on it. Without a large institutional
investor, that project woul d not have been able to progress in the way that it did and
the civil works on those projects would have taken much longer. But the superannuation
scheme still had to invest in that project, alongside other smaller commercial investors,
because it was rest ricted in having a controlling interest.
So what this bill does is it would allow strategic ownership where State ownership
of a project is useful for the public good, and that was something that the National
Government believed in at that point. Building up our services that are available for all
New Zealanders and increasing people’s access to capital and increasing businesses’
ability to get things done by having an institutional framework where investment was
possible in those kinds of large -scale projects actually enabled business to be able to do
what it needed to do and it enabled the building of houses in a way which let hundreds,
if not thousands, of first -home buyers move into what is now a thriving area of the
northwest of Auckland.
My point here is that this is a sensible change, but this is also a change which is
grounded in Labour values: that the State should take a role in strategic assets, which
enables business to thrive, and that the State should take a role in making sure that
ordinary New Zealanders have the infrastructure and the services that they rely upon to
thrive. The Superannuation Fund is a key part of that, and may we always have this kind
of cross-partisan belief in its value to all New Zealanders.

items.speaker: NANCY LU
items.text: I stand before you to take this to take this split call to support
the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests)
Amendment Bi ll at its second reading. This bill, in my opinion, is an essential step
forward in the evolution of the New Zealand Superannuation Fund because it aims to
repeal and replace the current restrictions that limit the fund’s ability to take a controlling
interest in entities.
At its core, when I read this amendment, it seeks to empower the fund by removing these
limitations, thereby granting the Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation the ability to
take a controlling interest in a variety of entities. This change is not merely administrative;
3018         NZ Super. & Retire. Income (Controlling Interests) Amdt Bill 1 May 2024
it is a transformative shift that aligns our Superannuation Fund with global best practices
and that, essentially, positions it to capitalise on significant investment opportunities here,
in New Zealand, and also around the world.
The landscape of global investment is rapidly evolving. Internationally, sovereign
wealth funds are increasingly directly engaged with markets, exerting influence to steer
business towards a more sustainable, ethical, and responsible practice. So by allowing the
Guardians to take a controlling interest, we are actually aligning ourselves with progressive
trends around the world to ensure that our fund is not a passive spectator, but a proactive
participant in shaping the future of our investment.
Moreover, this amendment bill is about enhancing the economic opportunities for
New Zealand. So by expanding the scope of our potential investments, the Guardians
will have access to a broader array of partnership opportunities that bring not only
financial returns but a strategic benefit for our economy. Whether it’s in technology,
renewable energy, rural land, infrastructure, or healthcare, having the ability to take a
controlling stake ensures that the fund can secure a meaningful influence in these ma jor
key sectors, fostering innovation and growth. So, ultimately, I believe we are providing
a better future for all New Zealanders and their superannuation.
This bill also champions, really, the integration of ESG —environmental, social, and
governance—criteria in investment decisions, because it enables the Guardians to hold a
controlling interest as they equip them with the leverage needed to encourage companies
to invest in more sustainable practices. This is an approach that aligns with global
standards, and it also resonates very strongly with the values of our society.
I support this bill because we are endorsing a vision —a vision of having a more
dynamic, influential, and responsible fund that would only bring our fund in line with the
best practices in the world. So I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: INGRID LEARY
items.text: It’s a great privilege to stand here and speak
about the Cullen fund as somebody who whakapapas politically to that great man Sir
Michael Cullen, who was the MP for St Kilda electorate, which became Dunedin South and
then in turn became Taieri. So I’m sure he is smiling upon us today, seeing the collaboration
across the House, and also perhaps giving his nod of approval to the logical next step in the
evolution of the fund, which has matured and proven its track record.
I’d like to speak on three things, really. One is about the track record but also the fa ct
that we probably do need to make this move to secure the sustainability of the fund, and,
thirdly, that we have mitigated the risks that might have presented in a way that I think
we can step forward confidently.
The fund was set up and the Act came in in 2001. In the South, we are known for our
fiscal prudence, and, certainly, Sir Michael was. I think it was very foresighted not only
to have the fund but also to have the section 59 caveat to manage the growth of the fund
and the risks to ensure that it would reach a state where it could then take that next step,
which is where we are today. I’ve also seen, having had the privilege of previously being
the chair of the Finance and Expenditure Committee in the previous term, the excellent
stewardship of th e Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation, which gives me
confidence that this is the right way forward.
But we do actually need to do this, as well. People have talked about our ageing
population. That is one pressure on the fund. There was also even talk  and, in fact,
campaigning from National and ACT about wanting to raise the superannuation
eligibility age to 67. So by taking this step, we can at least put that conversation to bed
for a while, hopefully, because, certainly, out and about in my electorat e, where
25 percent of the population are over the age of 60, that is the last thing that they want
to hear. In fact, if we look at Māori life expectancy, which has an aggregate gap of seven
1 May 2024       NZ Super. & Retire. Income (Controlling Interests) Amdt Bill 3019
years, that puts that superannuation even further out of reach fo r some people who will
never get to realise it.
It is also about deepening our capital markets, and I think that the risks around that
have been managed. In fact, if we look at capital markets, we can have the investment
lens, but can also look geopolitically. The more resilient and self -sustaining we are, the
less we have to rely on other global big players in getting pulled in different directions.
So there are really good resilience reasons why we would want to bolster this fund. The
risks around perhaps the difference between public and private elements of investment
have been very tidily cleaned up so that there would be no public reporting requirements
into private companies and no public obligations.
Two things I would like to speak on beca use they’ve come up in the debate. One is
around ethical investing, and, certainly, it is a growing practice in investing. I do think that
having looked at the Superannuation Fund and having also interrogated while sitting on the
Foreign Affairs, Defence a nd Trade Committee some investment elements around
investment into New Zealand—and looking at supply chain issues, in particular—it is not
