always easy to see if ethical investing is occurring and to safeguard against that, and that is
why the Labour Party was working on modern slavery legislation. I have seen, though, that
the frameworks with guardians of this fund —the Guardians of New Zealand
Superannuation—are very robust, and when issues come up, they do tend to pick up on
them very quickly. So there were good management controls over that.
There has also been a discussion about what people seem to be perceiving as mutually
exclusive ideas about high-return investing and social impact investing. While I agree it
is not wise to be prescriptive in investing , I do think those things are not necessarily
mutually exclusive, and I’d like to tip my hat to the man of the night —the Hon James
Shaw, who had his valedictory —because he certainly understands this area. It is a
growing area where investment can be made t hat can have really good capital value for
domestic markets, can also achieve social purposes, and can also maximise profit, and
I think we need to be aspirational, but certainly not to legislate around that.
So, with those words and tipping my hat again t o the late Sir Michael Cullen —that
fantastic man who has created this visionary fund —it’s been a pleasure to speak to it.
I look forward to us taking this leap into a high-growth future.

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Tom Rutherford. I was looking
for David MacLeod, actually, but he’s not here.

items.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD
items.text: Wow, he’s a bit of a silver fox—
Mr MacLeod —but I don’t pretend to be him one bit. I do sense the irony in having
the youngest member of the Government stand and speak on this piece of legislation, but
I’ll do it with—

items.speaker: Ingrid Leary
items.text: Oh, are you talking about me?

items.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD
items.text: No, no, I’m was talking about me —talking about me. But
I’ll do it with good grace and a lot of detail because it’s good to see some bipartisanship
across the House—

items.speaker: Celia Wade-Brown
items.text: More than two.

items.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD
items.text: More than two what?

items.speaker: Steve Abel
items.text: Bipartisan.

items.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD
items.text: Oh, partisan support across the House. Hey, I learnt
something—there we go. It’s good to se e that taking place this evening in support of
this bill in the legislation previously led by the previous Government. It was picked up
by the Minister of Finance and our Government and is being transitioned through.
That’s really, really pleasing to see.
3020         NZ Super. & Retire. Income (Controlling Interests) Amdt Bill 1 May 2024
I thought, actually, before I talk about the purpose of what the bill is aiming to achieve,
let’s talk about the background. Let’s talk about why we’re here in the first place, discussing
it, and then we’ll get into the purpose.
Section 59 of the Act currently requires the Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation
to use their best endeavours to avoid having the New Zealand Superannuation Fund take a
controlling stake in any entity. The original policy rationale for the control restriction was
that the New Zealand Superannuation Fund’s purpose was to get exposure to investments
and not to own businesses. If the Government wished to take ownership of businesses, it
would have a policy rationale for doing so.
Now, the New Zealand Superannuation Fund was also s till developing its
investment practices, and when it was set up and established in 2001 by the Labour
Government at that time, direct controlling investments were uncommon within the
global practice of investment management by sovereign wealth funds. Amen dments
in 2015 partially removed the restriction, allowing the Guardians to create and control
fund investment vehicles.
Now, that’s the background. That’s the context for why this House is today progressing
this bill through the second reading, with the full support of every party, which is very, very
pleasing to see. The purpose now is that the bill is repealing and replacing current sections
59 to 59B of the Act, and the amendments will remove the restriction on the New Zealand
Superannuation Fund and allow it to take a controlling stake in entities in the future. The
Guardians invest Government contributions into the Superannuation Fund, which is a
global portfolio of investments that will help pay for the increased cost of universal
superannuation payments in the future.
Now, as the youngest member on the Government benches, I can sense the irony about
the decision that we’re making here today when I’m standing to speak, but I can also see
why it is so valid that we’re making this decision. If I look at my—

items.speaker: Dan Bidois
items.text: It will pay for your retirement.

items.speaker: TOM RUTHERFORD
items.text: It is —it will help pay for my retirement. That’s a bit of a
long way off, but, yeah, we’ll see.
If I look at my personal electorate of the Bay of Plenty—not Hamilton, but the Bay of
Plenty electorate—we’ve got a median age of 40.2 at the moment, which is above the national
average of 37.4, and 18.5 percent of our population is aged over 65. Often, we were tarnished
with the brush of being the town for newlyweds and “nearly deads”, but I would say that we
are changing the landscape and we are filling the gaps in between. It is a wonderful
community for us to live in, and this amendment bill will have wider ramifications for our
Bay of Plenty community.
As my colleague Catherine Wedd said in her speech earlier, from the electorate she’s
representing in Tukituki—the fruit bowl, as she often refers to it—by the late 2050s, over a
quarter of New Zealand’s population will be aged over 65, and that is very stark. It’s
something we have to consider and we have to prepare for, and know that we’ve got things
in place to manage and mitigate it and undertake it.
So this bill confirms the allowance for the Guardians to hold a controlling interest in
a business. The select committee noted that the bill will allow the Guardians to take a
controlling interest in more active operating companies. I looked through the report
back from the Finance and Expenditure Committee in August of last year on the
New Zealand Superannuation a nd Retirement Income (Controlling Interests)
Amendment Bill, and when they went out for submissions, they received seven from a
mix of organisations and individuals. Four submitters gave full or qualified support for
the bill, while two were opposed, and o ne offered no opinion.
The recommendations from the select committee back to the House was that they did not
recommend any changes to the bill as introduced on the basis of the submissions they
1 May 2024       NZ Super. & Retire. Income (Controlling Interests) Amdt Bill 3021
received. Nevertheless, some submissions related to key issues that they thought merited
further discussion, and I thought about this part around benefits and risks of removing the
restriction on controlling interests.
The select committee in reporting back to the House has said that they “understand
that the main benefit of removing the restriction on controlling interests would be to allow
the Guardians to invest directly in a wider range of investment opportunities in New
Zealand, where such opportunities are relatively few. It would give the Guardians more
flexibility when entering and exiting a holding, providing additional capital to investee
entities, or influencing board and shareholder decisions on, for instance, ESG matters
(environmental, social, and corporate governance). Removing the restriction would als o
enable the Guardians to use simpler ownership structures, and take fuller advantage of
investment opportunities. On the other hand,” the select committee noted, “one potential
risk of this change is that it might compromise the Guardians’ independence from public
or ministerial pressure.”
So I wanted to dive into that a little bit deeper to see what the select committee said
could be some ways to mitigate that. They said that an example of what might occur could
be that “allowing the NZSF to take control ling stakes might lead to pressure to bail out
distressed New Zealand companies.”
The select committee understood “that this risk was considered when the Act was first
developed [in 2001], and the following protections were included to mitigate it: Section
58(2) of the Act requires the Guardians to invest the fund on a prudent, commercial basis.
The Board of the Guardians is responsible for the Fund’s performance, and for ensuring
that the Fund invests in a commercial manner irrespective of ministerial or p ublic
pressure.” The other part is “Section 64(1) and (2) of the Act provide that the Minister
can give only non -binding directions to the Guardians regarding the Government’s
expectations of the Fund’s performance, including as to risk and return. Further , the
Guardians’ board is appointed at ‘arm’s length’ from the Minister, via nominations from
a separate nominating committee, with each board member required to have substantial
expertise in the management of financial assets.”
This is a way of mitigating  the difference and not having undue pressure from
Ministers or anyone else on the Guardians and their board. I think it’s really clear that the
bill distinguishes between the Guardians as a Crown entity, and the Guardians as a
manager and administrator of the New Zealand Superannuation Fund.
Allowing the Guardians to hold controlling interests will have a limited impact on
competition with other market investors because the size and scale of the fund’s direct
investments differentiates them from the market, where there are few domestic investors of
this scale. The Guardians provide depth to the market for large capital investments. They are
truly long-term investors and can withstand short-term fluctuations in valuation.
Removing the control restriction w ill enable the Superannuation Fund to access a
wider group of viable investment partners and opportunities, particularly within New
Zealand. With the Guardians having a reputation of having world-leading environmental,
social, and governance (ESG) practice s, it will have a strong commitment to using its
influence as a shareholder to encourage companies to integrate ESG into their decision
making and to report on their ESG risks.
It is a pleasing night to gain support for a bill across this House from every  political
party. The New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests)
Amendment Bill is receiving the support of this House, and I’d like to commend it to
the House.
Motion agreed to.
Bill read a second time.
3022 Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill 1 May 2024
IMMIGRATION (MASS ARRIVALS) AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon ERICA STANFORD
items.text: I present a legislative
statement on the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: That legislative statement is published under the authority of
the House and can be found on the Parliament website.

items.speaker: Hon ERICA STANFORD
items.text: I move, That the Immigration (Mass Arrivals)
Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
This bill addresses legal risk to the safe and effective management of a potential mass
arrival. That risk is that the current 96 -hour deadline to obtain a group warrant of
commitment does not afford the members of a group enough time to receive adequate
legal repre sentation. Therefore, a warrant hearing may need to be held without legal
representation for those affected, which would breach their fundamental human right to
natural justice under the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act.
This bill makes minor and technical changes to our border settings, addressing the risk that
a mass arrival could not be processed appropriately. The likelihood of a mass arrival coming
to New Zealand does remain low, but none the less it is very real. I am aware that, as has been
reported in the media, a number of attempted ventures have been made in the past on the basis
of clearly stated intentions to come here. The pressure and scale on resources needed to
manage an arrival would be instant and significant, necessitating robust legislation  to
underpin our preparation. I consider these risks are unacceptable.
New Zealand must be prepared to manage an irregular maritime mass arrival and
ensure the rights of those are upheld should one occur. Ignoring the risks to our courts
and immigration sy stems, to the national security of our country, and especially the
risks to the migrants involved, would be irresponsible. This is a practical, pragmatic bill
that is intended to enable us to manage a mass arrival, should one occur, in a safe and
secure manner that ensures the human rights of the people concerned are protected, and
ensures the security of New Zealand’s communities are also protected.
I want to talk briefly about the select committee process. Though I was not on the
Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee in the last Parliament, I am aware of a
number of misunderstandings leading to misgivings about the bill that surfaced during the
select committee stage. The most significant misunderstanding that I want to be really clear
about is that  detention is not synonymous with imprisonment. There appears to be an
assumption that the provision set out in the bill and in fact the provision set out in the Act
as it currently stands would amount to arbitrary and automatic detention in prison. That is
not true. Neither in the current Act nor in this bill. There is no—and has never been—any
expectation that a mass arrival group would be held in a prison.
Officials informed me that they have identified a range of locations that might be used
to hold mem bers of a mass arrival group should one arrive, the primary one being the
Māngere Refugee Resettlement Centre, but also including managed isolation and
quarantine - style facilities and other accommodation providers. It would simply not be
appropriate or reasonable to grant visas and waive members of a mass arrival group off
into the community. That would lead to negative outcomes for both members of a mass
arrival group and New Zealanders in the community. Our response is predicated on safety
and efficiently accommodating them and ensuring that they can receive the dedicated
wraparound support that they will no doubt need.
I also want to note that the Ministry of Justice and its New Zealand Bill of Rights Act
analysis of the bill confirmed that the provisio ns in the bill do not amount to arbitrary
detention and do not unreasonably infringe on migrants’ human rights.
1 May 2024 Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill 3023
Some submitters said that the solution was simply to resource Immigration New Zealand
(INZ) and the courts and refugee lawyers better to manage the risks to natural justice. This
is incorrect and fundamentally misunderstands the risk. Primarily, it would not address the
fact that 96 hours is insufficient time for the migrants concerned to locate legal
representatives, brief them, have them be represented before a relevant judge, and to have
the judge take those representations into account when determining the group warrant of
commitment application. We are aware of only a limited number of lawyers in the country
qualified or experienced enough to adequately represent a mass arrival group, and that is
entirely out of our control. No matter how much additional funding we give INZ for such a
situation, it would not impact the number of lawyers available. Importantly, also, it would
be inappropriate to have that level of resource sitting around just in case there was a mass
arrival of possibly hundreds of people. New Zealand just does not operate on the scale
necessary for such resourcing.
Apart from anything else, we’re talking about very vulnerable pe ople who will have
undertaken a treacherous journey and who, on arrival, are likely to be exhausted at best
and may be in need of urgent medical and mental health attention. They are unlikely to
be in the best condition, and to be engaging with legal repre sentatives, or, in fact,
finding out where the accommodation services are in the community, is not a situation
we want to be in .
The bill’s provisions will enable the responsible judge to be confident that members of
a group have been given the time to have their voices heard by legal counsel, so the judge
can properly consider the migrants’ situations and views.
Other submitters suggested that we were acting contrary to our international
obligations. I also want to wholeheartedly contest this situation. The refugee convention,
international organisations, and the 2012 United Nations High Commissioner for
Refugees (UNHCR) guidelines on detention make it clear that there must always be a
process for receiving asylum seekers safely and securely. That’s precise ly what this bill
does. However, I want to assure submitters that I have heard you. Your feedback has been
valuable, and I am currently considering advice on whether any further changes could be
made to make more explicit the safeguards that already exist in our legal frameworks and
Immigration New Zealand procedures.
Before I finish, I want to just briefly touch on our standing internationally. New
Zealand has always strongly supported an international rules -based system, with the UN
at its heart. This is reflected in our enduring commitment to upholding human rights,
especially the rights of our most vulnerable who arrive in New Zealand. This is also
reflected in our strong support for UN institutions, such as the Security Council, the
Human Rights Council , and the Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees. In
particular, when managing asylum seekers, we always strive to act in a manner
consistent with international best practice and uphold the rules set up by the UNHCR,
such as those set out in the 2012  guidelines on detention. This legislation, with the
changes that I’ve proposed, will bring us even more in line with these guidelines and
put us ahead of many countries in the world, with respect to upholding the human rights
of those involved. Accordingl y, I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The question is that the motion be
agreed to.

items.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Labour is committed to an
immigration system that treats asylum seekers with dignity and that respects our obligations
under international law. We accept that there needs to b e a system for mass arrivals in
New Zealand. As the Minister outlined, while this is not something that it likely to occur
with any regularity, it is a known risk. The bill as it is in front of the House at the moment
fixes some of the unworkable aspects o f the law that was previously passed under the
3024 Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill 1 May 2024
National Government in 2013, and it is designed to ensure that there is a workable system
in place to process a group of asylum seekers and ensure their rights are respected in the
event of a mass arrival.
We acknowledge, as the Minister has, the refugee and human rights communities, who
are opposed to this bill and who did make strong submissions at the select committee process.
We want to state here in the House that we take the submissions that they made an d the
concerns that they raised extremely seriously.
There are a few changes that the Minister has alluded to and ones we would expect to
see in the mass arrivals bill to support it further. We had an unusual situation where the
select committee did not a gree to support the bill moving forward under the last
Parliament. So although we understand these changes are coming, they’re not currently
reflected in the way they usually would be in the bill at this stage. So the changes that we
would expect would be to establish that prior to a warrant of commitment being issued
and a member of the mass arrival group being detained —that that would have to be
approved by the chief executive under section 330 of the Act. But that would not be able
to be in a prison or a  police station—addressing some of the major concerns that were
raised by submitters about this bill.
Additionally, if there was to be a detention, there are some safeguards that we think
should be included within this bill. That includes establishing cle arly why the detention
was necessary, that it would be for the shortest amount of time possible and the least
restrictive necessary to achieve the outcomes, how the proposed location of the
detention meets the Government’s obligations under the New Zealand  Bill of Rights
Act—and I won’t go through all of these things because I think they were well covered
by the Minister. But it includes the safeguards that she alluded to, and they were ones
that we would expect to see in a bill.
We would also be open to further improvements of this bill at committee stage, if they
could be agreed, because we do take seriously the need to minimise the detention and to
make sure that any detention is subject to judicial oversight. It was Labour in Government
that commissioned the Victoria Casey KC review of the detention of asylum seekers in
prison in response to Amnesty International’s advocacy, and we accepted all of her
recommendations. We will also be actively working, and I know that our spokesperson
on immigration, Phil  Twyford, is keen to work closely with the Minister to consider
the further safeguards that may be needed to protect—

items.speaker: Hon Erica Stanford
items.text: I spoke to him tonight.

items.speaker: CAMILLA BELICH
items.text: —yeah, fantastic—asylum seekers. Some people may question
the need for a mass arrivals arrangement, and while it may be a low-probability scenario, it
is not zero probability. Because of that, we do accept that this legislation is needed in some
form, but, as I said, we are very concerned to make sure that the very serious human rights
concerns that were brought up by very respected groups in New Zealand are taken seriously
and mitigated, and that the human rights of asylum seekers are protected as much as they
possibly can be while at the same time we’re dealing with a quite unprecedented situation
that may occur in New Zealand. So we will be supporting this bill at this reading. However,
our support through its further stages through the House is dependent on the bill meeting the
very high standards that, hopefully—and I understand that we do—we share across the House
in relation to making sure that the human rights of those asylum seekers are upheld.
It’s a matter we take extremely seriously. We will be considering the amendments to
the bill at committee stage very seriously and, as I said, working really hard to make
sure that, hopefully, we can come to a situation where the bill is not seen in the light that
it has been seen by many of these very important human rights organisations that we
have heard from in New Zealand.
1 May 2024 Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill 3025
RICARDO MENÉNDEZ MARCH (Green) : Let’s make it really clear: this is the
Labour Party and the National Party colluding to push forward an anti - asylum seeker bill
that is grounded on very little evidence that there’s actually mass arrivals about to come to
this country, and while I am pleased to see the Labour Party somehow having a backbone
and some morals around the need to change this bill, the previous Labour Ministers that
enabled this bill to be pushed forward did not show any of these concerns when they
introduced it.
So, by nature, I just want to say to the Labour Party that they have enabled this bill
to be put forward to the House, and the Minister should not be so dismissive of the fact
that Amnesty International, Asylum Seekers Support Trust, Community Law, Council
for Civil Liberties, the Red Cross, World Vision, Refugee Family Reu nification Trust,
the Refugee Council of New Zealand, the Office of the Human Rights Proceedings, the
Human Rights Commission, and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
all either fully oppose this bill or could not support the bill in its curr ent state, showing
that there was very little, inadequate consultation with organisations that directly work
with asylum seekers.
I don’t have confidence that the Minister —and the Minister did not express whether
she had, herself, sought feedback from aff ected communities and people with lived
experiences who could actually speak to experiences of detention, who could speak to
issues around human rights. So we’re really concerned that this bill is continuing to go
forward without a pause and a review guide d by affected communities and by experts.
We note that when the bill was initially introduced, there was little to no consultation
with affected communities, and, in fact, many of the submitters noted how this bill
caught them by surprise and that many of them actually were not expecting something
of such degree in terms of potentially undermining the human rights of asylum seekers
to be put forward in this way.
I think I want to pick up on a few submitters and I wanted to pick up on Amnesty
International’s submission which talked a little bit about the right to liberty and security of
the person. What they noted here—because it’s, again, really important to be really clear
about what this bill ultimately is intended to do, which is to broaden the powers to detain
asylum seekers. They noted concerns around how this “expands the detention regime for
people seeking asylum.” and they also noted, importantly, that “International and domestic
law establishes that everyone, regardless of nationality, citizenship or migration status, has
the right to liberty, including protection from arbitrary arrest and detention and the
enjoyment of their personal security.”
Many submitters also noted how the move towards widening the powers of detention
without actually better resourcing, for example, the judicial system; to resource the
community organisations who actually support asylum seekers is, basically, the wrong
way around. I mean, one should be looking at resourcing the judicial system first,
looking at resourcing thos e community organisations first, before even thinking about
detaining asylum seekers, many of whom are escaping some of the most harrowing
situations that we will never experience here in Aotearoa, should we be lucky; we have
not had the experience of havi ng to go through genocide, through wars in Aotearoa. So
I think it’s really important to put into context the kinds of realities that people —who
could, in theory, arrive by boat to Aotearoa —would have had to experience, and they
deserve to be treated with respect and dignity.
The submitters also noted —and from my own engagement with constituents —that
many of the community organisations and, you know, the Māngere Refugee Resettlement
Centre, are already quite stretched in terms of resources and capacity. So to just assume that
without additional resourcing to our resettlement centres, that they can just be thrown there
or to hotels—actually at a time where hotels barely show capacity to host people seeking
3026 Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill 1 May 2024
emergency housing—just feels deeply unrealistic. Additionally, many submitters noted—
and you know, we look forward to any potential amendments from the Minister that may
address this—that it’s not enough to take the Minister at her word around the kinds of
facilities that will be used to detain people because there’s nothing in this bill that actually
adequately clarifies the kinds of facilities that would be used.
So while I take the Minister’s intent that her goal is to use the Māngere Refugee
Resettlement Centre or hotels, actually the bill, in and of it self, doesn’t create enough
clear protections to ensure that those facilities are adequate and that they’re actually used
responsibly when they are in place. So that is something that’s important to note because,
effectively, the bill as it is would still weaken and create another class of asylum seekers
who, technically, have reduced rights. And I think that’s also really important to note
here, about how we are, effectively, creating a whole other class of asylum seekers who
would be treated yet differently.
I also wanted to note the concerns from submitters around the rights of children. Some
submitters noted that, actually, children should not be detained for the actions of their parents.
No matter whether you sugar-coat the detention centre as a hotel or as the Māngere Refugee
Resettlement Centre, this bill would enable the detention of children who are part of whānau
seeking asylum, and that is deeply, deeply concerning. And we don’t think there’s enough
safeguards in this bill to adequately protect children either.
If we look at some of the reporting that at least we know is available, I would really
welcome the Minister to elucidate to Parliament on what these other risks are that she’s
aware of that exist, because what’s in the public domain is peopl e who have expressed,
when asked, intent that they would like, in theory, to reach this country. But, actually, I
think if you ask many asylum seekers if they’d like to, in theory, come to Aotearoa, I think
many of them would say yes, because they know that it is a country that is not experiencing
a genocide at this point, or war, and that it is seen internationally as a relatively safe
country compared to the types of nations that asylum seekers would be coming from. So,
yes, of course if you were to ask s omeone, they would say “Yes”, but we can’t use
those reports as justification for this bill. So the Minister needs to be more upfront and
specific around the types of threats that are present to justify this bill.
And I note that the National Party flip -flopped on this bill. In fact, when they were
in Opposition, they had concerns around this bill, and now they seem to be fully on board
with it. But they haven’t actually given us adequate justification for their change
of position.
I think, ultimately, what this bill will do is worsen the rights of asylum seekers. It will
create yet another category. It will leave children completely at risk of being detained, which
is not in line with the international reputation that we would want. Additionally, without
commitment to adequately resourcing the judicial system and our community centres, none
of the problems that the Minister claimed that she wanted to solve will actually be addressed.
So that’s another concern.
I think the Greens will be calling for this bi ll to be paused completely to address
other more important issues that actually make life harder for asylum seekers, to focus
on Victoria Casey’s report recommendations and I think, at the end of the day, take the
lead from the experts. I don’t think the M inister’s an expert on asylum seeker issues.
Most of us are probably not in this House, but there are plenty of people and
organisations who work directly with asylum seekers who could guide us on what could
be a human rights - compliant legislation, a rig hts-enhancing legislation that would
support asylum seekers, that would support human rights, and this bill does absolutely
nothing towards that. All that it does is actually create yet another category of asylum
seekers, and, therefore, we think that this is a rights-diminishing bill rather than a rights-
enhancing bill, as it has been for trade.
1 May 2024 Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill 3027
Ultimately, we can’t just throw statements such as “We want to treat asylum seekers
with dignity or respect.”, while, at the same time, introducing bills that dimi nish those
very same rights that we like to think of as upholding the dignity of asylum seekers. So
the Green Party won’t be supporting this bill. We’ll be looking forward to the committee
of the whole House debate to see what kind of amendments the Minist er is introducing,
and we call on the Labour Party to actually also take heed of the experts who are calling
for this bill to be paused and to be stopped, and to withdraw their support from the bill so
that they can at least come to the right side of history, rather than continue to enable a bill
that will diminish the rights of asylum seekers.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: Sorry, Mr Speaker, I see there’s no microphone
here. So thank you, Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I can hear you well now.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: Ha, ha! Thank you. I’m taking this call on behalf of
ACT to support this bill in its second reading. This is the Immigration (Mass Arrivals)
Amendment Bill.
I note that this bill went through its first reading in the last term and then it was reported
back as well in the last term —the term that I skipped. The Foreign Affairs, Defence and
Trade Committee did the job on this bill. They did what they were supposed to do—they
heard from submitters—and I note that there were 322 submissions on this bill. In my view,
322 submissions means that there was a significant  interest in this legislation —and
22 submitters appeared online and spoke to their submission. So I want to acknowledge all
those submitters and thank them for their contributions. I also want to thank the previous
Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee.
As we have heard, this is actually a very small and technical amendment, what this bill
does—it is to the Immigration Act 2009. As we have heard before, this is 96 hours’
provision which is there for the judges to make a decision on warrants of commit ment
that, in this bill, is to be changed to—because 96 hours is four days, that is to be changed
to seven days. And if it was not reasonably practicable for the District Court to
consider an application for a mass arrival warrant of commitment within seve n days, it
says the detention could be extended by a judge to 28 days.
Now, I use this term “detention” as we have heard from the Minister of Immigration
that there were some concerns in the select committee about this term. It has been made
clear that “de tention” doesn’t mean putting people in prison. I fully understand what
submitters said, because what was really interesting to see in the select committee
process—as I read in the report —is that most of the submitters actually opposed this
legislation. The reason for that was that humanitarian angle: that was about how women,
children, disabled people will be treated, because the impression was that they will
be locked up in some kind of prison. That has been made very, very clear that the
“detention” word in here doesn’t mean they will be in some kind of prison.
Now, it’s also important that we take note that, yes, geographically we are far from
other countries. The risk is lower—or negligible, we can say—because in the report I note
it said that “since 20 15, 85 asylum seekers were detained in New Zealand [detention]
facilities.”, and that “no asylum seekers have been detained in custody since early 2020.”
The report was done in mid-2023, and I assume that this is still true and we haven’t had
any asylum se ekers since early 2020 detained in custody. Looking at that, the risk
definitely is quite low for us, but this is about futureproofing and we are talking about
people—those who might randomly arrive here, and this is random maritime arrivals that
we are talking about.
On the other hand, I would like to address a few points that the Green member Ricardo
Menéndez March raised in his speech. He talked about respect and dignity. Of course, respect
and dignity is important for these people—those who arrive here—and that is why we believe
3028 Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill 1 May 2024
that there needs to be sufficient time allowed to them to have legal representation. This is
about natural justice that we want to have in our provisions.
But what I don’t agree with is the member says that this is like creating “another class”.
I don’t think it is about another class. Definitely, they are a different group of asylum
seekers because we do get refugees through our United Nations High Commissioner for
Refugees system and those refugees are already qualified as refugees—so we accept them
as refugees. But these people, when they arrive here, then we have to go through the
process to see if they are real refugees.
We cannot just continue to accept everybody who arrives at our borders through this
kind of mechanism—accept them as refugees and start giving them citizenship—because
that way, we will be sending a very wrong signal out there to people, and people will start
taking risks—risking their life—to arrive here.
We also know—this is a fact—that when people get on to these boats, they don’t come
here for free. There is somebody who is charging a big amount of money to put these
people on a boat because they really want to leave that country and come to a country that
they desire to be in.
So the ACT Party has decided to support this bill in the second reading, and we really
look forward to the committee of the whole House. This is not about creating another
category; this is about making sure that we treat asylum seekers as asylum seekers and
not treat people differently, and not try to create classes within refugee classes. But also
making sure that we are not encouraging people getting on a boat and coming to New
Zealand, expecting that, as soon as they arrive here, they will be stamped as refugees and
they will get citizenship. So, with that, I would like to say that we are supporting this bill
in the second reading. Thank you.

WEDNESDAY, 1 MAY 2024 
The Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
KARAKIA/PRAYERS 
SPEAKER: Almighty God, we give thanks for the blessings which have been bestowed 
on us. Laying aside all personal interests, we acknowledge the King and pray for guidance 
in our deliberations, that we may conduct the affairs of this House with wisdom, justice, 
mercy, and humility for the welfare and peace of New Zealand. Amen.  
RESIGNATIONS 
Hon James Shaw, Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand 
SPEAKER: I wish to advise the House that I have received a letter from  the 
Hon James Shaw, resigning his seat in the House, with effect at 11.59 p.m. on Sunday, 
5 May 2024. 
VISITORS 
United States of America—American Council of Young Political Leaders 
SPEAKER: I’m sure that members would wish to join me in welcoming visiting 
delegates from the American Council of Young Political Leaders on their exchange here 
in New Zealand. They are present in the gallery.  
PETITIONS, PAPERS, SELECT COMMITTEE REPORTS, AND 
INTRODUCTION OF BILLS 
SPEAKER: No petitions have been delivered to the Clerk. No papers have been delivered 
for presentation. Select committee reports have been delivered for presentation. 
CLERK:  
 Report of the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee on the 
Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill 
 report of the Finance and Expenditure Committee on the Standard Estimates 
Questionnaire 2024/25. 
SPEAKER: The bill is set down for  second reading and the report on the Standard 
Estimates Questionnaire is set down for consideration. No bills have been introduced. 
ORAL QUESTIONS 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Question No. 1—Prime Minister 
1. Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS (Leader of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister: 
Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON (Prime Minister): Yes. In particular, I stand by 
the Government’s “ phone away for the day” policy, which is so popular with parents 
and students and schools —and with great feedback from people like the Hornby 
High School head boy, Khush Patel, who said the ban “has helped students focus 
more academically”. Cameron Stone, the principal of Stratford High School in the 
mighty Whanganui electorate, said, “It’s an awesome, overwhelming success for us.” 
I have to say, I am proud to lead a Government that makes the changes that we need to 
ensure our kids are well set up for a great future, because we’re getting our country back 
on track. [Interruption] 
2942 Oral Questions 1 May 2024 
 
SPEAKER: Wait on—just wait on. It’s worth noting that when you watch this replay 
on TV, the person speaking is clearly audible, with a bit of mumble in the background, so 
most of that is denying the House an answer, as opposed to the general public. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins: Point of order, Mr Speaker. I suspect there would have been 
a little less noise had half of the Government benches not been looking at their phones 
during the Prime Minister’s answer. 
SPEAKER: Well, that’s an interesting point but not a point of order. 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: Point of order, Mr Speaker. If the House didn’t 
hear it, I’m happy to repeat it. 
SPEAKER: Thank you for your generous offer. I’m not interested in hearing it again, 
so can we please have the supplementary from the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins : What will the average weekly cost be  to families, due to 
the Government’s decision to no longer fund half-price public transport for people under 
the age of 25? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON : It depends on their circumstances, but if the 
member would like to put the question in writing, we’ll get him a proper answer. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins : Why isn’t he aware that, using the National Party’s own tax 
cut calculator, someone in their early 20s that takes the bus each day and earns the average 
wage could be worse off by more than $70 a fortnight as a result of that change? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: Well, look, I thank the member for their concern 
about that constituent, but what I’d say is that help is on the way, because we ar e going 
to deliver low and middle income tax relief to hard-working Kiwis. These are the people 
that the Labour Party used to care about but have long forgotten. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins: Is he aware that parents will now need to pay more to get their 
under-13s to school as a result of that change, while his Government is also threatening 
to cut the school lunch programme that could see those same parents $33 a week, per 
child, worse off? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: I’d just say to that member, again, help is on the 
way to low and middle income New Zealanders doing it tough in a cost of living crisis 
created by that member’s previous Government. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Could I ask the Prime Mi nister as to whether people in 
Auckland would be catching the bus each day if light rail had been built as Labour 
promised? 
SPEAKER: That’s one of those interventions that is interesting but not worthy of 
a question. 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: That’s an excellent question. Can I answer that 
question? 
SPEAKER: Well, unless you’ve got responsibility for the failure of a previous policy, 
I don’t think so. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins : Will the $2.9 billion of tax cuts for landlords result in lower 
rents, given Trade Me reporting that rents have surged 8.3 percent since last year? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON : This Government is committed to putting 
downward pressure on rents, and we are bringing the brightline test back from 10 to two 
years; we’re making sure we restore interest deductibility and we get the balance of laws 
right between tenants and landlords. But what I’d say to that member is we are not going 
to see a $170 per week increase in rents, as we saw under his administration. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins : So will rents decrease as a result of this Government’s tax 
cuts for landlords? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: The series of actions we’re taking in the rental 
market will put downward pressure on rents. 
1 May 2024 Oral Questions 2943 
 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins : What does he think best reflects his promised laser -like 
commitment to tackling the cost of living: higher public transport costs, his Government’s 
new drivers tax, higher costs for prescriptions, higher rents, higher fuel prices, higher rates, 
lower pay increases, or higher unemployment? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: Well, I can tell you there is a series of things that 
this Government is doing to focus on lowering the cost of living and lowering inflation. 
We’ve got the Reserve Bank focused on a single target of fighting inflation, we’ve 
actually made sure we’ve introduced our Family Boost policy  to give families that are 
struggling with childcare costs some support and subsidy, and we’re making sure that 
we’re going to give tax relief in this Budget for low and middle income working 
New Zealanders. We’re serious about lowering inflation, and isn’ t it good that inflation 
hit 4 percent—the lowest it’s been for three years—we’re on our way. 
Question No. 2—Justice 
2. TĀKUTA FERRIS (Te Pāti Māori —Te Tai Tonga) to the Associate Minister 
of Justice : What evidence, if any, does she have that reintroducing three -strikes 
legislation will reduce crime in Aotearoa? 
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Associate Minister of Justice): The Ministry of Justice has 
previously produced an evidence brief suggesting that reintroducing the three -strikes 
legislation in New Zealand has the potential to reduce crime. US studies on similar laws 
have shown reductions in both minor and serious viol ent crimes, along with decreased 
arrest rates among offenders with previous strikes. The tougher sentences for offending 
that this regime will introduce for second- and third-strike offenders will ultimately keep 
serious repeat violent and sexual offenders  off the street and prevent them from 
victimising more New Zealanders, including Māori. 
Tākuta Ferris: What is the response to the 2018 report by then Prime Minister Bill 
English which called out Aotearoa’s high rates of incarceration for being based on dogma, 
not evidence, and criticised policies such as three strikes for being a retributive rather 
than restorative approach to crime based on unsupported claims that prisons can solve the 
problem of crime? 
Hon NICOLE McKEE: My response to that report is that we have made constructive 
changes to the regime that will be implemented to ensure that those serious repeat violent 
sexual offenders are off our streets and our communities are safe. The reason for that is 
because this Government is committed to restoring law and order to our communities. 
Tākuta Ferris: Does she accept the findings from research from the United States in 
2022, where this law was modelled from, that showed three strikes has no measurable 
deterrent effect, that it disproportionately locked up African Americans, and that it had 
no impact on lowering crime rates at all? 
Hon NICOLE McKEE: The Ministry of Justice has previously produced an evidence 
brief which cited US studies  showing similar three -strike laws have reduced serious 
violent crimes and reduced arrest rates for offenders who had received a first or second 
strike. I think what is really important here is that we have taken learnings from the 
previous regime and we will be introducing a new regime which goes about making sure 
that our communities are kept safe. [Interruption] 
SPEAKER: Excuse me—just wait for the quiet. Away you go. 
Tākuta Ferris: Tēnā koe e te Pīka. What is your response to the unequivocal majority, 
the 99 percent of submitters at select committee who represented most of the law 
associations of this country, that this bill is not fit to be passed into the House, should be 
done away with, and something new put in place? 
2944 Oral Questions 1 May 2024 
 
Hon NICOLE McKEE : I invite those people, when they actually see the bill once 
it’s produced, to use the select committee process to give us their new version of what 
they think about it. 
Todd Stephenson: Have we seen an—[Interruption] 
SPEAKER: Hang on, wait on. Questions will be asked in silence. 
Todd Stephenson: Thank you, Mr Speaker. 
SPEAKER: Well, actually, no —the question can be audible, but everyone else can 
be silent. 
Todd Stephenson: Ha, ha! My sign language is not very good. [Interruption] 
SPEAKER: OK, just wait. We’ll go quiet. 
Todd Stephenson : Have we seen an increase in violent crime justifying the need 
for a new three-strikes regime? 
Hon NICOLE McKEE: Well, yes, we have. Since Labour came into power, we have 
seen a 33 percent increase in violent crime, resulting in an increased number of 
victimisations. The new and improved three -strikes regime will hold serious repeat 
violent and sexual offenders to account, get them off the street, and prevent more Kiwis 
from becoming victims of crime. 
Todd Stephenson: What is the Minister’s intention with the three-strikes policy? 
Hon NICOLE McKEE: To restore law and order by getting repeat violent and sexual 
offenders off the streets. We’re sending a message to the criminals: think twice, because if 
you commit a violent or sexual offence, you’re going to be going away for longer. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Is it the Minister and the Government’s position that the 
greatest proportion of victims of violent crime are Māori, and, rather than make a 
sociological example, we’re going to do something about it? 
Hon NICOLE McKEE: Yes. Regardless of who a person is, if they commit a serious 
sexual or violent offence they are going to be locked up. But what we do need to take 
into account is the disproportionate portion of Māori and Pasifika people who are 
victims of crime.  It’s very disappointing to see representatives from Te Pāti Māori not 
even speaking about the victims of crime but more about cuddling and cotton -wooling 
those criminals instead.  
Question No. 3—Finance 
3. DANA KIRKPATRICK (National —East Coast)  to the Minister of Finance : 
What challenges has she faced in putting together this year’s Budget? 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS (Minister of Finance) : Well, aside from the state of the 
economy that was left to us— 
SPEAKER: Hang on; I think just tone it down just a little bit. Actually, quite a bit —
quite a bit. And similarly over here. That’s right, the person in front of you.  
Hon NICOLA WILLIS: As I pointed out in the Budget Policy Statement, one of the 
biggest challenges for this year’s Budget is that the previous Government left 
behind multiple initiatives with time -limited funding that was about to expire. At the 
half-year update in December, Treasury identified nine instances of these fiscal 
cliffs where, in each case, the costs of continuing funding were $100 million more 
over the forecast p eriod. Fiscal cliffs made the future fiscal track look superficially 
better, but this practice was misleading and left any incoming Government facing very 
difficult funding decisions.  
Dana Kirkpatrick: What is the biggest fiscal cliff the Government has faced? 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS : The biggest fiscal cliff in Budget 2024 was time -limited 
funding for Pharmac. The previous Government gave Pharmac additional funding of $350 
million for the 2023-24 fiscal year to purchase new medicines and widen access to some 
that were already funded, but this expires on 30 June and there was no funding set aside 
1 May 2024 Oral Questions 2945 
 
for future years. My colleague David Seymour announced on Monday that Budget 2024 
will extend this additional funding and, critica lly, make it permanent. That will be 
welcome news to people who rely on these medicines, but we have had to find the 
$1.77 billion cost of this from within our operating allowance because the previous 
Government did not put one cent towards it.  
Hon David Seymour: Can the Minister confirm that official advice to Ministers from 
Pharmac is that had the pre-existing budgeting been applied, Pharmac would have needed 
to de-list medicines that New Zealanders had every expectation of receiving but had no 
money put aside for under the previous Government? 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS: Well, yes, I can confirm that and I will recall vividly— 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins: Point of order, Mr Speaker. I’ve just been contemplat ing the 
member’s question. He’s actually asking a hypothetical question about what would have 
happened under a re -elected Government; what a re -elected Government may have 
done. The current Minister has no responsibility for what an alternative Government 
may have done.  
SPEAKER: A very good point. I was actually listening to the question and starting to 
think along those lines. But I think the question could be asked in a different way, and as 
long as it’s relatively brief, how about giving that a go? 
Hon David Seymour: May I speak to the point of order. 
SPEAKER: I’ve just ruled on it. 
Hon David Seymour: Well, I may be able to clarify the intention behind the question.  
SPEAKER: No, no, have another go at the question, please. 
Hon David Seymour: With pleasure. Can she confirm that under the fiscal track that 
was set for this Government after it assumed office, it received advice from Pharmac that 
if it didn’t fill in the fiscal cliff for medicine funding, it would have to de-list medicines that 
New Zealanders relied upon, because the fiscal track, the budgeting that this Government 
inherited, had not put money aside to pay for— 
SPEAKER: Hang on. The question was good up to “advice”.  
Hon NICOLA WILLIS : One of the meetings I will recall vividly for the rest of my 
political career is one that I attended with Minister Seymour, where we asked health officials 
and Pharmac officials how New Zealand could possibly be in a position where they were 
saying to us that unless we found $1.77 billion, they would be forced to start de -listing 
essential medicines upon which New Zealand relied. I remember that meeting vividly 
because what I saw in the eyes of their officials was what I felt, which was abject horror at 
the situation the previous Government was prepared to leave Pharmac in. 
Dana Kirkpatrick: What reaction has the Minister seen to this announcement? 
Hon NICOLA WI LLIS: Well, I have seen one commentator —who should know 
better—describe this $1.77 billion commitment to continue funding much -needed 
medicines as “fiscal jiggery-pokery”. Personally, I would reserve the term “fiscal jiggery-
pokery” to describe the practic e of funding medicines for one year only and then taking 
it away again. I think that is being highly misleading to New Zealand, and I would expect 
much better from the Labour health spokesperson, Ayesha Verrall. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins : Point of order, Mr Speaker. I wonder whether you could 
indicate to us where the ministerial responsibility for that last answer lies. 
SPEAKER: Well, you have to go to the question itself, which was—sorry, it just slips 
my mind for a minute. But the response—I’ll tell you what, I’m going to have to look at 
it afterwards. Sorry about that. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins: Speaking to the point of order, Mr Speaker, the question was 
absolutely in order. Ministers aren’t responsible for the questions that they are asked; they 
are absolutely responsible for the answers that they give. Nicola Willis has a repeated 
history of giving answers  that fly directly in the face of rulings that you have given 
2946 Oral Questions 1 May 2024 
 
repeatedly since you took up your tenure as Speaker—but she’s also very clever because 
she puts the dig in right in the last few words. I think there should be some ability for the 
member who’s the subject of the answer to ask questions in response to that. 
SPEAKER: It’s a novel idea and, actually, is, interestingly, the whole purpose of 
question time. So the Opposition will organise their supplementaries to, obviously, give 
effect to that! But what I can say is that I do look at question time. It’s not an easy thing 
to, day after day, watch question time twice. But I do so where there are, particularly, 
questions that are under question from the Opposition—largely to see just where the lines

Question No. 10—Children 
10. TAMATHA PAUL (Green —Wellington Central)  to the Minister for 
Children: Does she agree with official advice that military-style bootcamps are “likely to 
be detrimental to young people with a history of abuse”; if not, why not? 
Hon KAREN CHHOUR (Minister for Ch ildren): First of all, I’d like to say I 
disagree with the member’s interpretation of the advice, as asked in the question. If you 
take the advice as it was stated in full, which said, “Traditional bootcamp models of strict 
discipline are likely to be detrimental to young people with a history of abuse and family 
violence.”, yes, I do agree. The advice also noted that programmes which include 
elements of counselling and have primary focus on rehabilitation are significantly more 
effective. The programme that this Government is working on will have a military -style 
component with a rehabilitative and trauma - informed care approach. This is not just 
about consequences for young people who offend but actually showing them that they 
have it within themselves to  turn their lives around. It will give them the tools and the 
encouragement that they need to do so. 
Tamatha Paul: Does she think the 86 percent reoffending rate of the last military -
style activity camps is a sign of success, and, if not, wh y is she repeating this failed 
experiment that causes traumatised young people more harm? 
Hon KAREN CHHOUR: The military-style academies in the Military-style Activity 
Camp programme were run between 2010 and 2016. An evaluation of that programme 
showed positive results, with improvements in attitude and motivation of the young people 
to address their offending. However, it was also found that the lack of robust support once 
the young person left the programme meant that the improvements in outcomes were not 
realised to the extent that they might have been. That is why the programme that this 
Government is working on is going to have a rehabilitative and trauma - informed care 
approach, alongside the military approach to ensure that these young people will receive 
the full wraparound support they need to turn their lives around. 
Tamatha Paul: Does she think it’s acceptable to experiment on young people when 
there is a wealth of evidence on what works to reduce youth crime? 
Hon KAREN CHHOUR : What I don’t find acceptable is not giving these young

different agencies, looked around to different programmes, taken learnings from those

communities. This is about reducing harm in our communities and making sure that our

Question No. 11—Building and Construction 
11. Dr VANESSA WEENINK (National —Banks Peninsula) to the Minister for 
Building and Construction: What announcements has the Government made in building 
and construction? 
Hon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction): The Government is 
bringing for ward a review of earthquake -prone buildings to provide greater certainty 
for Kiwis. While this review is under way, all current remediation deadlines will be 
extended by four years. Of course, some building owners who have already planned on 
making improve ments will be in a position to continue this work, motivated by 
considerations such as private insurance arrangements or the ability to tenant buildings. 
But we have heard, in many cases across New Zealand, that buildings were not going 
to be remediated wi thin the original time frames anyway because of barriers such as 
crippling cost and heritage status.  
Dr Vanessa Weenink: Why are these changes needed? 
Hon CHRIS PENK : Our Government is focused on rebuilding the economy. The 
current earthquake -prone building system was put in place in 2017 in good faith and 
required buildings considered to be earthquake -prone to be remediated before set 
dates. Nearly 500 deadlines are set to expire over the next four years. Counci l and 
building owners across New Zealand have told me and other Government members that 
many buildings will not meet their deadlines due to the costs involved being much 
higher than originally contemplated and further complicated by heritage rules and 
other artificial constraints affecting residential housing.  
Dr Vanessa Weenink: What impact will these changes have? 
Hon CHRIS PENK : These changes from the review, or at least the ones we 
contemplate will flow from the rev iew, we hope will provide considerable relief across 
New Zealand. The earthquake -prone building rules impact the entire country —not just 
Wellington—in small -town New Zealand and larger cities alike. Without change, an 
increasing number of buildings could s it empty and derelict, which would have a 
devastating effect on the economy across New Zealand —again, in a multitude of 
different built environments.  
Dr Vanessa Weenink: What are the next steps? 
Hon CHRIS PENK: Cabinet  will soon agree to terms of reference for the review, 
which will be informed by feedback from a wide range of affected New Zealanders.

extension to remediation deadlines .

Hon NICOLA WILLIS (Minister of Finance): I move, That the House take note of

I want to start with a message for New Zealanders: things are tough right now. Inflation 
has been too high for too long. It is almost three years since inflation went above 3 percent 
and gave rise to a cost of living crisis that was prolonged a nd has now gone on for some 
years. Interest rates have risen very high to try and fight that inflation —higher than they 
would have had to if there had been a Government that was doing its bit to take the fuel off 
the inflation fire. Now, with high inflatio n and high interest rates, there are many New 
Zealanders who are struggling, and we are seeing the results of that. 
We are seeing those New Zealanders who’ve switched to a higher mortgage interest 
rate now lacking the choices they once had about what they spend in their households. 
We are seeing that in the small businesses who now have fewer people walking through 
their doors with the money to spend on the goods they provide and the services they 
sell. We are seeing that with the young entrepreneurs who may have once taken a risk and 
taken a big loan out on something but now look at that high official cash rate and take

a pause. All of that means that today we saw the unemployment numbers climb up. And

single member of this Parliament who would ever, could ever, welcome that. Because we 
feel—deeply—the pain that occurs in a family when a New Zealander who wants a job 
cannot get one. That is why, on this side of the House , we take so seriously our duty to 
sound economic policies that will strengthen the fundamentals of this economy so that 
New Zealanders can get ahead once more. 
We understand that the lifting of the unemployment rate this week is not the 
consequence of a d ecision taken yesterday or the week before. It is the build -up of

Hon ERICA STANFORD (Minister of Education): This Government is aspirational 
and ambitious for our nation’s kids, and academic achievement will be at the heart of 
everything that we do to ensure that we have a world-leading education system. Because 
all Kiwi kids —including tamariki Māori —deserve a world -leading education,  to be 
literate and numerate, and to have the knowledge and skills they need to take on the world 
or be great iwi leaders. 
Education is the key to change lives and alter the course of one’s future, to break cycles 
of intergenerational poverty and dependenc e, but our current educational results are 
failing too many kids in this country. Nearly 10,000 students in 2022 left without a 
qualification, and 40 percent of those year 10 and 11 learners who sat the foundational 
literacy and numeracy assessments were unable to pass last year. These results show that

kids from low socio-economic homes—overrepresented by our Māori tamariki—are well 
overrepresented in these statistics. The equity gap is worse here than in any country that 
we compare ourselves to. These are  the very kids who need access to a world -leading 
education to change their circumstances the most, and in New Zealand, our great 
egalitarian society, your means determine your destiny; 42 percent of our kids at year 8

kids, 14.5 percent are at curriculum for maths at the end of intermediate. This very much 
reduces their ability to experience success at high school. 
I want every single child in this country to experi ence educational success, academic

knowledge-rich curriculum that lays out the knowledge and skills that should be taught 
each year; implementing evidence-based structured literacy, maths mastery—approaches 
that are grounded in the science of learning about how the brain learns; implementing 
consistent methods of regular progress monitoring so that teachers and parents know 
where their students and kids are at; we will develop the workforce of the future including 
leadership development pathways, because we know the single most important thing in 
our education system is our teachers and our leaders; we will target effective learning 
support interventions for students with additional learning needs; and key to all of this is 
data and evidence to drive improvement.  
Make no mistake: this represents a fundamental shift in education that our kids

teaching of knowledge and skills in a consistent manner. And this, combined with the

of their Māori kids at curriculum for reading, after two years: 67 percent. T hose are the 
evidence-based policies we will be putting in place to make sure our tamariki Māori are 
getting every single opportunity they need to succeed in this world, and it will be a

Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts) : Thank you, Mr Speaker. When we 
boil it all down, one of the central purposes of G overnment is to keep their citizens safe 
from threats, allowing them to go about living free and productive lives. During their 
previous six-year tenure, Labour shirked this responsibility and failed Kiwis. Everyday 
citizens were exposed to harm daily and their individual freedoms were being constantly 
1 May 2024 General Debate 2961 
 
attacked by others. During that time, we saw a ram raid epidemic explode, with the 
number of ram raids committed increasing by 465 percent in just two years as of March 
2023. We saw liquor stores and corner d airies being raided by machete -wielding thugs,

over our streets. In the case of Ōpōtiki last year, we saw the takeover of a whole town.

and order. They told us they want appropriate consequences for serious repeat violent 
and sexual offendi ng, and this new regime will provide it. Three strikes is this

back from the Finance and Expenditure Committee in August of last year on the

Amendment Bill, and when they went out for submissions, they received seven from a 
mix of organisations and individuals. Four submitters gave full or qualified support for 
the bill, while two were opposed, and o ne offered no opinion.  
The recommendations from the select committee back to the House was that they did not 
recommend any changes to the bill as introduced on the basis of the submissions they

received. Nevertheless, some submissions related to key issues that they thought merited 
further discussion, and I thought about this part around benefits and risks of removing the 
restriction on controlling interests. 
The select committee in reporting back to the House has said that they “understand 
that the main benefit of removing the restriction on controlling interests would be to allow 
the Guardians to invest directly in a wider range of investment opportunities in New 
Zealand, where such opportunities are relatively few. It would give the Guardians more 
flexibility when entering and exiting a holding, providing additional capital to investee 
entities, or influencing board and shareholder decisions on, for instance, ESG matters 
(environmental, social, and corporate governance). Removing the restriction would als o 
enable the Guardians to use simpler ownership structures, and take fuller advantage of 
investment opportunities. On the other hand,” the select committee noted, “one potential 
risk of this change is that it might compromise the Guardians’ independence from public 
or ministerial pressure.”  
So I wanted to dive into that a little bit deeper to see what the select committee said 
could be some ways to mitigate that. They said that an example of what might occur could 
be that “allowing the NZSF to take control ling stakes might lead to pressure to bail out 
distressed New Zealand companies.” 
The select committee understood “that this risk was considered when the Act was first 
developed [in 2001], and the following protections were included to mitigate it: Section  
58(2) of the Act requires the Guardians to invest the fund on a prudent, commercial basis. 
The Board of the Guardians is responsible for the Fund’s performance, and for ensuring 
that the Fund invests in a commercial manner irrespective of ministerial or p ublic 
pressure.” The other part is “Section 64(1) and (2) of the Act provide that the Minister 
can give only non -binding directions to the Guardians regarding the Government’s 
expectations of the Fund’s performance, including as to risk and return. Further , the 
Guardians’ board is appointed at ‘arm’s length’ from the Minister, via nominations from 
a separate nominating committee, with each board member required to have substantial 
expertise in the management of financial assets.” 
This is a way of mitigating  the difference and not having undue pressure from 
Ministers or anyone else on the Guardians and their board. I think it’s really clear that the

manager and administrator of the New Zealand Superannuation Fund.  
Allowing the Guardians to hold controlling interests will have a limited impact on 
competition with other market investors because the size and scale of the fund’s direct 
investments differentiates them from the market, where there are few domestic investors of 
this scale. The Guardians provide depth to the market for large capital investments. They are 
truly long-term investors and can withstand short-term fluctuations in valuation.  
Removing the control restriction w ill enable the Superannuation Fund to access a 
wider group of viable investment partners and opportunities, particularly within New 
Zealand. With the Guardians having a reputation of having world-leading environmental, 
social, and governance (ESG) practice s, it will have a strong commitment to using its 
influence as a shareholder to encourage companies to integrate ESG into their decision 
making and to report on their ESG risks.  
It is a pleasing night to gain support for a bill across this House from every  political 
party. The New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) 
Amendment Bill is receiving the support of this House, and I’d like to commend it to 
the House.

3022 Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill 1 May 2024 
 
IMMIGRATION (MASS ARRIVALS) AMENDMENT BILL 
Second Reading 
Hon ERICA STANFORD (Minister of Immigration) : I present a legislative 
statement on the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill. 
DEPUTY SPEAKER: That legislative statement is published under the authority of 
the House and can be found on the Parliament website. 
Hon ERICA STANFORD : I move, That the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) 
Amendment Bill be now read a second time. 
This bill addresses legal risk to the safe and effective management of a potential mass 
arrival. That risk is that the current 96 -hour deadline to obtain a group warrant of 
commitment does not afford the members of a group enough time to receive adequate 
legal repre sentation. Therefore, a warrant hearing may need to be held without legal 
representation for those affected, which would breach their fundamental human right to 
natural justice under the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. 
This bill makes minor and technical changes to our border settings, addressing the risk that 
a mass arrival could not be processed appropriately. The likelihood of a mass arrival coming 
to New Zealand does remain low, but none the less it is very real. I am aware that, as has been 
reported in the media, a number of attempted ventures have been made in the past on the basis 
of clearly stated intentions to come here. The pressure and scale on resources needed to 
manage an arrival would be instant and significant, necessitating robust legislation  to 
underpin our preparation. I consider these risks are unacceptable. 
New Zealand must be prepared to manage an irregular maritime mass arrival and 
ensure the rights of those are upheld should one occur. Ignoring the risks to our courts 
and immigration sy stems, to the national security of our country, and especially the 
risks to the migrants involved, would be irresponsible. This is a practical, pragmatic bill 
that is intended to enable us to manage a mass arrival, should one occur, in a safe and 
secure manner that ensures the human rights of the people concerned are protected, and 
ensures the security of New Zealand’s communities are also protected. 
I want to talk briefly about the select committee process. Though I was not on the 
Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee in the last Parliament, I am aware of a 
number of misunderstandings leading to misgivings about the bill that surfaced during the 
select committee stage. The most significant misunderstanding that I want to be really clear 
about is that  detention is not synonymous with imprisonment. There appears to be an 
assumption that the provision set out in the bill and in fact the provision set out in the Act 
as it currently stands would amount to arbitrary and automatic detention in prison. That is 
not true. Neither in the current Act nor in this bill. There is no—and has never been—any 
expectation that a mass arrival group would be held in a prison. 
Officials informed me that they have identified a range of locations that might be used 
to hold mem bers of a mass arrival group should one arrive, the primary one being the 
Māngere Refugee Resettlement Centre, but also including managed isolation and 
quarantine - style facilities and other accommodation providers. It would simply not be 
appropriate or reasonable to grant visas and waive members of a mass arrival group off 
into the community. That would lead to negative outcomes for both members of a mass 
arrival group and New Zealanders in the community. Our response is predicated on safety 
and efficiently accommodating them and ensuring that they can receive the dedicated 
wraparound support that they will no doubt need. 
I also want to note that the Ministry of Justice and its New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 
analysis of the bill confirmed that the provisio ns in the bill do not amount to arbitrary 
detention and do not unreasonably infringe on migrants’ human rights. 
1 May 2024 Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill 3023 
 
Some submitters said that the solution was simply to resource Immigration New Zealand 
(INZ) and the courts and refugee lawyers better to manage the risks to natural justice. This 
is incorrect and fundamentally misunderstands the risk. Primarily, it would not address the 
fact that 96 hours is insufficient time for the migrants concerned to locate legal 
representatives, brief them, have them be represented before a relevant judge, and to have 
the judge take those representations into account when determining the group warrant of 
commitment application. We are aware of only a limited number of lawyers in the country 
qualified or experienced enough to adequately represent a mass arrival group, and that is 
entirely out of our control. No matter how much additional funding we give INZ for such a 
situation, it would not impact the number of lawyers available. Importantly, also, it would 
be inappropriate to have that level of resource sitting around just in case there was a mass 
arrival of possibly hundreds of people. New Zealand just does not operate on the scale 
necessary for such resourcing. 
Apart from anything else, we’re talking about very vulnerable pe ople who will have 
undertaken a treacherous journey and who, on arrival, are likely to be exhausted at best 
and may be in need of urgent medical and mental health attention. They are unlikely to 
be in the best condition, and to be engaging with legal repre sentatives, or, in fact, 
finding out where the accommodation services are in the community, is not a situation 
we want to be in . 
The bill’s provisions will enable the responsible judge to be confident that members of 
a group have been given the time to have their voices heard by legal counsel, so the judge 
can properly consider the migrants’ situations and views. 
Other submitters suggested that we were acting contrary to our international 
obligations. I also want to wholeheartedly contest this situation. The refugee convention, 
international organisations, and the 2012 United Nations High Commissioner for 
Refugees (UNHCR) guidelines on detention make it clear that there must always be a 
process for receiving asylum seekers safely and securely. That’s precise ly what this bill 
does. However, I want to assure submitters that I have heard you. Your feedback has been 
valuable, and I am currently considering advice on whether any further changes could be 
made to make more explicit the safeguards that already exist in our legal frameworks and 
Immigration New Zealand procedures. 
Before I finish, I want to just briefly touch on our standing internationally. New 
Zealand has always strongly supported an international rules -based system, with the UN 
at its heart. This is reflected in our enduring commitment to upholding human rights, 
especially the rights of our most vulnerable who arrive in New Zealand. This is also 
reflected in our strong support for UN institutions, such as the Security Council, the 
Human Rights Council , and the Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees. In 
particular, when managing asylum seekers, we always strive to act in a manner 
consistent with international best practice and uphold the rules set up by the UNHCR, 
such as those set out in the 2012  guidelines on detention. This legislation, with the 
changes that I’ve proposed, will bring us even more in line with these guidelines and 
put us ahead of many countries in the world, with respect to upholding the human rights 
of those involved. Accordingl y, I commend the bill to the House.

agreed to.
